subsubtopic: LOSS OF CODFISH ON ACCOUNT OF SCARCITY OF SALT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Thursday last the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Browne), while I was out of the city, asked a question which was directed to the Prime Minister, about a shortage of salt in Newfoundland.

My advice from the chairman of the Newfoundland fisheries board is that some shortage did exist, but its extent was exaggerated. In a wire from him this morning he confirms that there is no shortage at present. I am informed that in some localities in these bays, fish had struck into the shore traps earlier than usual. In some areas the local merchants had not adequate supplies on hand, and in trying to effect a quick distribution of salt to these areas the shortage of small boats for transportation delayed supplies. My information this morning is that stocks are generally ample and well distributed geographically, through the action of the trade itself. In other words, there is no general shortage of salt in Newfoundland at the present time. There is difficulty in getting it from one place to another as speedily as they would like, but other supplies are coming in gradually.

speakerposition: topic
maintopic: STATEMENT OF MR. MALIK AS TO NEGOTIATIONS FOR CEASE-FIRE AND ARMISTICE

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of ihe Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: STATEMENT OF MR. MALIK AS TO NEGOTIATIONS FOR CEASE-FIRE AND ARMISTICE
speechtext:
In view of the extremely
important statement made by Mr. Malik on Saturday and since the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), who is in London, has commented on that statement in London, is the Prime Minister in a position to make any comments that would enlighten the house as to the attitude of the government toward this statement? May I say that I am not pressing for any statement, my question being prompted only by the fact that comments had been made in London by the Secretary of State for External Affairs.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: STATEMENT OF MR. MALIK AS TO NEGOTIATIONS FOR CEASE-FIRE AND ARMISTICE
speechtext:
I understand that some newspaper men in London put certain questions to the Secretary of State for External Affairs to which he replied. I have not had time to consider the replies carefully because I received the clippings just as I came into the house. There is no doubt that the Secretary of State for . External Affairs, like all the rest of us, regards that statement as an important development. It is one with which the United-Nations will no doubt be dealing expeditiously, and I think it might perhaps be convenient to put on the record of this house the statement made by the secretary general, Mr. Trygve Lie, which was in the following form:
In recent weeks, the qualified spokesmen of many' of,-the governments "whose forces are participating in the United Nations action in Korea, and I, as
Inquiries of the Ministry secretary general, have expressed hope for a military cease-fire in Korea in the vicinity of the 38th parallel. The delegate of the U.S.S.R., deputy foreign minister Jacob A. Malik, now has also expressed his hope for such a cease-fire.
The United Nations forces have been fighting in Korea to uphold peace and security under the United Nations charter. From the outset, the United Nations have made it clear again and again that the first step to the restoration of peace in Korea must be a cease-fire. Such a cease-fire should involve only the military arrangements necessary to stop the fighting and to ensure against its renewal.
I urge that negotiations for a military cease-fire now be entered into at the earliest possible date.
If such a cease-fire can be attained, the political issues involved in the restoration of peace and security in Korea can then be appropriately discussed in the competent organs of the United Nations.
I am further informed that Mr. Entezam, president of the general assembly, and also chairman of the good offices committee, has come from Washington to New York in order to be in touch with the representatives of the United Nations there and to take such immediate action as may be appropriate and to do so in the hope that this is a statement of a real desire to see a cease-fire and a withdrawal of opposing troops on either side [DOT] of the 38th parallel brought about at once.
I think hon. members would be interested to know that among the clippings I got was one referring to a radio broadcast in the capital of communist China reporting this statement of Mr. Malik and an editorial saying that if America was willing to stop the war she should bring in at once those just and reasonable measures for peaceful settlement which have been repeatedly proposed by the people's republic of China, the Soviet union, and other countries desiring peace.
Of course that statement was along the same line; even Mr. Malik's statement was much along the traditional line of having about fourteen minutes of violent vituperation and then a half a minute in which to make the statement that he thought the problem of armed conflict in Korea could be settled - at this time. That is the usual manner in which such proposals are put forward by the U.S.S.R., but we have had former experience of their violent vituperation having been followed by something which was really serious and intended to be effective. I hope this may prove to be another such example.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: STATEMENT OF MR. MALIK AS TO NEGOTIATIONS FOR CEASE-FIRE AND ARMISTICE
speechtext:
In view of the statement made by the Prime Minister, may I join in the hope which'he has expressed, and I am sure every Canadian will join with me. In view of the important part that Canada is bound to play in any discussion which takes place, and the desirability of achieving such a measure of

Inquiries of the Ministry unanimity as may be possible in this house, no matter what our views may be on other subjects, I urge the Prime Minister to keep us fully informed as to the developments, subject of course to such terms of secrecy as necessarily are associated with extremely important considerations of this kind.
As the Prime Minister has pointed out, the statement by Mr. Malik was hardly designed to make an impression of sweet reasonableness; nevertheless on this anniversary of the attack in Korea, I think we should bear in mind that the Russians have backed down on other occasions-as they did in Greece; as they did in Azerbaijan; as they did also in connection with the airlift to Berlin. Certainly I think all of us will hope that this is not merely a part of a sham peace campaign, but a genuine offer to terminate hostilities, which can certainly benefit no one, and which, if terminated, may be the beginning of a period during which, by the combined strength of the free nations, we may attain the measure of security for which we are all hoping.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: STATEMENT OF MR. MALIK AS TO NEGOTIATIONS FOR CEASE-FIRE AND ARMISTICE
speechtext: I may add that this morning the Secretary of State for External Affairs is conferring with Mr. Herbert Morrison, the United Kingdom foreign minister, and that our ambassador in Washington was in touch yesterday and is in touch today with the Secretary of State there. The language of this declaration is being carefully scrutinized, and there is no indication anywhere that it will be brushed off. It will be explored with a sincere desire, at least on our side, to have it produce some results.

maintopic: STATEMENT OF MR. MALIK AS TO NEGOTIATIONS FOR CEASE-FIRE AND ARMISTICE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to associate the members of this group with the remarks of the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition. The statement made on Saturday by Mr. Malik is one of exceeding importance, and whether or not its purpose is propaganda, the United Nations should now have sufficient experience, if that is the intention, to turn it back on the Soviet union. But perhaps its purpose is not propaganda. We should and do welcome the statement made by the secretary general of the United Nations. It must be the earnest hope of everyone that a cease-fire order may be possible. Once a cease-fire order is made, it is doubtful that the fighting would begin again.

speechtext: As I understand it, under some arrangement Canadian National Railways have been using the first twenty-five miles from Quebec on the way to Murray Bay. Will the minister say under what arrangement it has been using it in the past, whether on a basis of rental or otherwise?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS
subtopic: ACQUISITION OF THE RAILWAY OF QUEBEC RAILWAY, LIGHT AND POWER COMPANY
speechtext:
The arrangement was what is known as an "interline carrier" arrangement. That means that if the freight rate is $1, let us say, for an article moving over the Quebec Railway, Light and Power Company line, and the freight is carried three-quarters of the distance over the line of that company, seventy-five cents will go to the Quebec Railway, Light and Power Company and twenty-five cents to the C.N.R. It is pretty difficult to give the arrangement in detail, but I understand it is a common arrangement entered into between railways. When traffic is carried by one railway over the line of another, whether the traffic originates on that line or
Canadian National Railways whether it comes from other lines, the interline carrier arrangement is one which is pretty much standard between railways.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION ACT
subtopic: PROVISION FOR AUDIT OF PUBLIC ACCOUNTS, FINANCIAL CONTROL OF CROWN CORPORATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
This resolution, Mr. Chairman, seeks leave to introduce a bill to provide for the financial administration of the government of Canada, the audit of the public accounts and the financial control of crown corporations, and as I indicated, I should like to make this statement at this time.
Briefly stated, the purpose is threefold. In the first place, it is proposed to consolidate in one statute, in simplified, clarified and, where necessary, in amended form, the provisions relating to the financial organization and administration of the government of Canada and the audit of the public accounts, which are now included in the Department of Finance and Treasury Board Act, the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act and certain other statutes.
In addition, certain new provisions will be introduced which experience has shown are essential for the administration of the collecting, disbursing, borrowing, and accounting activities of an enterprise of such magnitude as the government of Canada.
In the second place, it is proposed to provide a statutory basis for the management and control of public stores similar in principle to that provided in the Department of Transport Stores Act. Thirdly, it is proposed to establish a more uniform system of financial and budgetary control, and accounting, auditing and reporting, for crown companies.
The Department of Finance and Treasury Board Act has been on the statutes in virtually unchanged form since 1869. The Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act has not been amended since 1931. The pronounced and rapid growth in the size and complexity of government business in recent years, and particularly in the war and post-war period, has shown the need for certain changes in the existing legislation. In bringing together in one statute the principal provisions of these acts relating to the financial organization and administration of the government, some obsolete and unnecessary provisions have been eliminated, and a number of amendments have been introduced.

Financial Administration Act
After this resolution is approved the bill will be given first reading. There will not be time for further action on it at this session, but it is the government's desire that the bill be given full and careful study, and by introducing it in the house at the present time it is hoped that hon. members and others interested will have an opportunity to consider fully its terms. When it is reintroduced at the next session of parliament in the autumn, it is the intention to refer the measure to the public accounts committee for detailed consideration; and it is our hope that by making it public at this time its consideration then may be facilitated.
Financial operations as extensive as those of the government would, under any set of circumstances, require an elaborate administrative organization. Day-to-day operations must be carried on smoothly and efficiently, and decisions based on accurate and current information must be made and executed without delay. This calls not only for a high degree of speed and technical efficiency in the collecting and disbursing processes, and in recording and classifying financial transactions; it also means that those who are required to make decisions must be in a position to do so promptly. Inevitably, in an enterprise of any magnitude, this involves some delegation of authority. However, the government's financial business must be carried on with full regard to the traditional relationships which exist under our parliamentary system of government between the legislature and the executive. With the substantial increase in the amount of public business which comes before it, parliament can no longer deal, as it once did, with the details of administration. However, the government is the executant of the will of parliament, and must look there for its authority, and a broad measure of control and accountability is both necessary and proper.
The working out of the precise degree of control that should be exercised raises many difficult problems, but I believe that when hon. members have had an opportunity to study the provisions of the bill in detail they will agree that a very real effort has been made to preserve for parliament the final word on those fundamental matters which are, and indeed which should be, for parliament alone to deal with. When authority has been granted to the executive a full measure of accountability has been assured. In short, the aim has been, by the proper delegation of authority, to achieve business efficiency in operations with full regard for the fundamental concepts of parliamentary sovereignty and executive responsibility.
One of the most important parts of the bill is the provision for the continuation of an

independent audit of the public accounts on behalf of parliament. The office of Auditor General, as we know it today, had its genesis in 1878, when provision was made for an examination of the accounts of Canada by an officer independent of the executive and responsible directly to the House of Commons. In succeeding revisions of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, the Auditor General's independence as a servant of parliament was carefully preserved. The present bill makes no change in this regard, except to remove the present rather anomalous requirement that the Auditor General shall, if so directed by the governor in council, examine the accounts of any branch of the public service before payment.
Although in practice in recent years the Auditor General has been called upon to undertake few pre-audits, it has seemed to us wholly inconsistent that, on the direction of the governor in council, he should be obliged to commit himself to the propriety of expenditures before payment. It is the statutory duty of the comptroller of the treasury, as an executive officer, to make the necessary prepayment examinations and satisfy himself that there is authority for proposed disbursements. To project the Auditor General into this administrative process is, I am convinced, wrong in principle, and for this reason it is not proposed to re-enact this provision in the bill.
The treasury board is an integral part of our machinery of government. The new bill will replace the main portion of the Department of Finance and Treasury Board Act, but provision will be made for establishing the department and providing a statutory basis for the board's existence and position as a committee of the privy council. It is proposed to provide a clearer definition of the board's powers and field of operations, to authorize it specifically to make regulations with respect to various financial matters and the administration of the public service, and, when authorized by the governor in council, to perform certain purely administrative duties now performed by the council.
One of the most pressing problems of central administration in recent years has arisen from the fact that council has been obliged to concern itself with a multiplicity of minor matters of purely administrative character. To relieve it of some of these routine matters, it is proposed to introduce a provision enabling it to authorize the treasury board to exercise a number of the administrative powers conferred on it-that is, the council- under the civil service and certain pension and superannuation acts. Not only will this result in a considerable reduction in the volume of work which now comes before council,

but it will enable many of these routine matters, which are referred to the treasury board before being considered in council, to be dealt with more expeditiously than in the past.
A number of new provisions are being introduced with respect to the collection, management and disbursement of public moneys. Most of them are of a technical nature relating to the mechanics of the financial processes, and are designed either to clarify existing legislation or to improve or simplify present administrative practices, and I think it would be more appropriate if they were explained in the committee stage of the bill. However, there are two or three of the proposed revisions which I believe are of more immediate interest to the house, and I should like to refer briefly to them. First, however, I might say that the provisions relating to the office of the comptroller of the treasury, which was established when the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act was amended in 1931, are being re-enacted in substantially unaltered form, with such additions as experience has shown are advisable.
Among the new provisions of the bill it is proposed to include specific provision making it clear that the Minister of Finance may purchase, hold and sell securities of Canada. The authority to invest balances of public moneys not immediately required for use has always been regarded as vested in the minister as part of his duties in managing the consolidated revenue fund. In placing the practice on a statutory basis the purpose is to give a clear definition of these powers as part of the general function of managing public moneys and the public debt, and to provide a direction as to the accounting treatment to be given profits and losses incidental to the investment operations.
Another new provision will relate to writing off uncollectible debts owing to His Majesty that have been outstanding for many years. At the present time there is no parliamentary authority to write off such debts, and considerable expense has been incurred by departments in maintaining records of -claims that are valueless. The problem of dealing with these uncollectible items has been considered from time to time by the public accounts committee, and hon. members will recall that in its third report last year the committee recommended that consideration be given to the establishment of a procedure whereby amounts which have been outstanding for the previous ten years could be written off. A procedure is now being proposed for dealing systematically with such bad debts of limited size, which I commend to the public accounts committee for its consideration.
Financial Administration Act
It is also proposed to include a clause to provide that when a guarantee has been given under the authority of parliament, any amount required to be paid under the terms of the guarantee may be paid without any further appropriation. I believe it is a matter of the utmost importance that when the government, in the name of His Majesty and under the authority of parliament, has given a guarantee, there should be no question that its terms may be implemented and any necessary payment made without delay.
Another important new feature of the bill is the proposal to establish a system for the control of public stores. The principle involved is not new. It is essentially that now followed under the Department of Transport Stores Act, but it has seemed desirable to provide more comprehensive legislation which may be applied to the stores of any department. Briefly stated, the proposed measure provides for the general regulation of the acquisition, custody and issue of departmental stores, and establishes the accounting machinery for financial control through the operation of revolving funds. It is not intended that a revolving fund should be established for every department, but for those departments where the requirements of several services financed from different appropriations may be met by centralized purchasing and warehousing practices, there should be substantial economies in the use of such funds. The use of revolving funds will be subject to the approval of parliament, possibly through the inclusion of an appropriate item in the estimates; and when a department has been authorized to operate a fund and the amount that may be charged to the fund at any time has been fixed by parliament, the department's stores investment will be limited to the amount authorized.
One of the important new parts of the bill is that providing for the control of the financial affairs of crown corporations. The crown corporation form of enterprise is not a new type of organization, but in recent years, as the work of government has become more complex, increasing reliance has been placed on it as the appropriate instrument for administering and managing many public services in which business enterprise and public accountability must be combined. In the schedules to the bill some thirty-three corporations are listed, engaged in activities ranging from the production of munitions and synthetic rubber to the provision of housing, transportation and broadcasting services. Apart from the Government Companies Operation Act of 1946, which applies only to certain crown companies incorporated under part I of the Companies Act, 1934,

Financial Administration Act there is no comprehensive legislation dealing with the financial operations of these enterprises and their financial relations to the government. In the present bill it is proposed to remedy thiis omission and to make systematic provision for the financial control of those crown corporations that are listed in the schedules of the bill and such others as may be designated by the governor in council as falling within the several categories established in the bill.
It is apparent from an examination of the acts under which the existing corporations were established that parliament has not granted all of them the same degree of independence and autonomy. Ultimate accountability to parliament has in all cases been a prime objective, but the way in which this has been achieved has varied widely. At the one extreme are those bodies which, as departments of government, are responsible for administrative, supervisory or regulatory services and are subject to more or less continuous day-to-day control and direction of the government or a minister, but which, for one reason or another, have been given corporate status. At the other extreme are those bodies that conduct lending and financial operations, or manage commercial and industrial operations involving the production of or dealing in goods or the supplying of services to the public, and are normally required to pay their own way. These proprietary corporations, as they are designated in the bill, have usually been given a considerable degree of managerial freedom, and such control as is exercised by the government or a minister may be compared to that of the equity shareholder of a business corporation.
Falling neither within the class of departmental corporations on the one hand, nor of proprietary corporations on the other, are those crown corporations which are created to manage trading or service operations on a quasi-commercial basis, or to undertake procurement, construction or disposal activities on behalf of the crown. These bodies, which we term "agency corporations", are normally dependent on appropriations to meet deficits, and it is this characteristic which suggests that they should be subject to somewhat more detailed financial control than are proprietary corporations.
It is proposed that departmental corporations will be governed as at present by the same provisions as are applicable to departments generally.
With respect to agency and proprietary corporations, it is proposed that the terms of the crown corporations part of the bill should
[Mr. Abbott.!

apply, but in the event of any inconsistency between the provisions of that part and any other act, it is specifically provided that the provisions of such other act shall prevail. The purpose is to lay the groundwork for uniform financial control and to legislate with respect to those matters which the present acts do not cover. At some future date the financial provisions of the special acts may be reviewed, but for the present it is proposed that they should continue to operate.
I will not attempt at this time to cover all the provisions of this part of the bill, but I might say that it is proposed that the annual capital budgets of both agency and proprietary corporations, as approved by the governor in council, should be laid before parliament. Provision will also be made for regulating the establishment of reserves and the treatment of surplus moneys; for enabling corporations to meet emergency requirements for working capital; and, in the case of agency corporations, for prescribing the conditions upon which they may undertake contractual commitments. It is also proposed to make provision for keeping proper books of account, for the preparation of financial statements and the submission of annual and other reports, and for auditing the accounts and financial transactions of corporations.
In the provisions relating to the appointment and reports of auditors of crown corporations it is proposed in some respects to override existing legislation. We propose to qualify the Auditor General for appointment as the auditor, or a joint auditor, of a crown corporation, in any case in which he is not now eligible for appointment, and to require the auditor to report on the financial affairs of the corporation in the terms specified in this bill.
In effect, the auditor is now being asked to examine the income and expenditure statement as well as the balance sheet, and to satisfy himself not only that transactions have been accurately reported, but that they do not exceed the powers of the corporation. In recent years the scope of the auditor's examination and the phraseology of his report have been subjects of serious consideration in the United Kingdom and in the United States, and in both countries within the past three or four years new forms of report have been introduced. This is a field in which professional accountants and auditors are well qualified to give advice, and, in seeking to develop a satisfactory form of audit certificate applicable to crown corporations, I would welcome an expression of views from accounting organizations and others professionally interested. The bill, as

I have indicated, will be reintroduced when the house meets again, in the autumn, and in the intervening time I should be pleased to receive and consider any recommendations or suggestions which may be submitted.
I think I have mentioned, Mr. Chairman, the more important aspects of the bill. There are a number of other proposed provisions, such as those relating to the management of the public debt, placing the government officers' guarantee fund on a statutory basis, and re-enacting the provisions of the Debts Due to the Crown Act, which will be repealed; but I think that it is more appropriate that these be explained in committee.
In bringing together in one place the provisions covered by the proposed bill, it will be possible to repeal a number of existing statutes which hon. members will find listed in a schedule to the bill.
I know, Mr. Chairman, that it is not customary to call the attention of the house to the work of departmental officers in connection with the preparation of legislation, but on .this occasion I feel impelled to depart from the usual practice and to mention the name of my deputy minister. In the preparation of this bill, as in so many matters of importance to this house and this country, Dr. Clark's contribution cannot be overemphasized, and I consider it fitting that I should record this fact.
I should like also to express my appreciation of the valuable and constructive advice and assistance which I and my officers have received from the Auditor General at every stage in the preparation of this bill. All of the suggestions proposed by Mr. Sellar have been worthy of, and have received, the most serious consideration, and many of them are embodied in the text of the measure covered by this resolution.
The bill will provide a more positive and effective regulation of financial transactions and public stores and property; it will ensure a more satisfactory control of the financial affairs of crown corporations, and it will enable parliament to receive a full accounting of the manner in which public moneys have been collected and spent. I commend the measure to the committee, and ask that the resolution be adopted.

When we were setting out the duties of the board, the provinces insisted that after any question had. been determined by the board it should be sent to the provincial governments for approval. That is what I am going to say. The matter of building the South Saskatchewan river dam would not be affected by that. When the board was set up-I am sorry I have not the exact dates this morning, but I sent for the letters in order to make up the return that is to be brought down; I believe it was several months ago, and I am not sure that it may not have been one or two years since we were first discussing the form of the water board for the three provinces. During that time, Manitoba, being the last to receive the water, naturally was much concerned as to whether the board was going to be able to make the final decision. So far as this government was concerned, we were quite prepared at that time to say that the board could make the final decision. But the provinces were not prepared to accept that, more particularly the province of Manitoba. I think Manitoba was fairly strongly supported by the other two provinces. Eventually we agreed to the board being set up with the undertaking that any decision reached would have to be approved by the governments of the provinces before it would become final.
There were no discussions then which would indicate that anybody was opposed to anything; it was only that they wanted the right to protect their own interests when it came to the time to deal with the matter. As I recall the correspondence, which will be on the file when it comes down and I think will verify what I am going to say, the only objection raised by the Saskatchewan government that could be called an objection was raised by the minister of agriculture on
Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act behalf of the government, in a letter written wishing to know, before they consented fully, whether or not sufficient water was being allowed to pass the boundary line of Alberta into Saskatchewan to fill up a dam such as the South Saskatchewan river dam and make water available to do the things that we were maintaining could be done. An attempt has been made to satisfy them on that point, and I really think they are satisfied.

I do not think I should attempt to prophesy as to what the decision of the government will be. Because of a remark made when the hon. member for Lake Centre was on his feet previously, I believe I should say that I do not think the decision or advice of the committee, no matter which way it may be, must necessarily be taken by the government. It is one of those cases that often arises. I myself, for example, have had more to do with this dam than anyone else. I instructed the engineers in the first place to study the possibility of building a dam on the South Saskatchewan river. For three or four years before anybody discussed the matter publicly we were discussing it from week to week in the department. Therefore I feel I am under some obligation personally to the taxpayers of Canada to say: If you are going to spend $68 million, you are going to get something for it.
As I said previously when we were discussing this matter, I am convinced that a lake in the middle of Saskatchewan would be a good thing, even if it did not produce any power or any water for irrigation at all; from some other points of view a lake there might easily be worth a great deal of money to the whole of Canada. But even so, I have been in politics for a long time, and I do not believe I have any white elephants hanging around yet; therefore I would prefer to be absolutely certain before asking the government of Canada to arrange to spend $68 million, together with $33 million of the province's money, to develop a project of this kind. I should like to feel absolutely certain, as near as one can, that it will be a success when it is built. I can hardly think of anything the committee can say which would make me more convinced than I am now.

This measure is entirely technical in nature and is designed to bring up to date the federal law relating to surveys of public lands coming under federal government jurisdiction. This revision is the outcome of changed conditions and of developments in modern surveying practices. A modification of the existing law has become necessary because of legislative changes in the last few years. The Dominion Lands Surveys Act has become inoperative because it applies to classes of lands coming under the old Dominion Lands Act, which was repealed last year and replaced by the Territorial Lands Act.
Three main changes are proposed in this new Canada Lands Surveys Act. First, the public lands to which it applies are redefined. Second, its provisions have been adapted to modern surveying practices. Third, the qualifications of surveyors have been restated.
As I have said, this bill, being purely technical in nature, should be non-controversial.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OP NATIONAL STANDARDS
speechtext:
The proposed act will replace the Dairy Industry Act, and it is made necessary by reason of the decisions of the supreme court and the judicial committee of the privy *council on the margarine reference. Consideration was given to whether it would be sufficient to amend the act in all its different sections in order to provide for the changes that were necessary because of those decisions, but on the advice of the Department of Justice new legislation has been drafted.
The main points of difference as compared with the present act are as follows: First, the manufacture and sale of dairy products will no longer be controlled. The provision in the act prohibiting the manufacture and sale of dairy products substitutes will be dropped. Second, the control of interprovincial and export movement of dairy products for which grades and standards have been established is added to the import control as provided for under the present act. In other words, the method of attack in connection with the enforcement of regulations having to do with dairy products is through control of the interprovincial and international sides of the handling of the product rather than through control of production and sale within a province.

Mr. Speaker, when one
o'clock was called I was about to proceed with a few remarks on the motion for second reading of this Criminal Code amendments bill.
On the motion for second reading the points we should discuss are those of principle. These annual batches of Criminal Code amendments that are brought forward every year include a number of clauses which may involve no particular point of principle but rather some point of procedure or of administration. On the other hand, by including in one bill all the suggestions which come to us from a variety of sources and concerning a variety of subject matters, all of which have to do in some way with crime and the administration of criminal law, we usually get, as we have in the present bill before us, a number of quite different principles that are involved in certain clauses of the bill.
Not only would it save a great deal of time of the house, but I believe it would make for a clearer discussion if, with the consent of hon. members, we could have the understanding that we go at once into committee. Then, in committee, as each of these principles is encountered, in the clause or group of clauses in which it is involved, perhaps I

Criminal Code
might be permitted to lead off with a statement concerning the principle of that particular clause or group of clauses. We might then have the understanding that debate would proceed upon that principle and the related sections, and we would conclude the debate on this principle before we opened another debate on the next principle and its related sections. If that is satisfactory I shall content myself in supporting the motion for second reading by indicating those clauses and groups of clauses in respect of which I suggest important principles arise.
First of all there are clauses 3, 4, 5, 6, 8 and 9, which establish an important new principle with regard to treason and sedition; and clause 18, which provides a new offence of sabotage. Then there is another group of clauses which deals with a general revision and consolidation of all those sections of the Criminal Code relating to the registration of pistols and revolvers, the principle of that particular group being that of modernizing these sections and making them applicable to present conditions.
The next group contains clauses 12, 16 and 20, which deal with offences relating to His Majesty's mail.
The next group in that connection with which there are certain important principles involved is that relating to what has been termed drunken driving.
A new principle arises also in clause 21, which has to do with a device which has been suggested to us by the Department of the Attorney General of Ontario to deal with the stamping out in that province of bookmaking and other gambling offences.
I believe we will make much better progress if we follow the course I have suggested. With that thought in mind I shall now terminate my remarks, and hope that we may have second reading at once.

I know some members are receiving a great many communications in regard to certain clauses of the bill. I am not greatly concerned about that, because I generally know the sources from which they come and the motives the people concerned have. But even there we should, I suggest, if we must err, err on the side of caution.
I suppose what I have said should have been said before Mr. Speaker left the chair. I am very sorry that this measure has come before us in this way at this late hour of the session. If the amendments are urgent, then we should have had them earlier; if they are not urgent, then I see no reason why they should hot lie over until the fall session.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
I think perhaps the principle involved in this clause is of sufficient importance to warrant my making a statement, which I shall try to keep as short as possible.
Section 74, subsection 1, paragraph (i) of the code as it stands at present provides that treason is assisting any public enemy at war with His Majesty in such war by any means whatsoever. The amendment that we are now considering broadens this definition by making it treason to assist any armed forces against whom Canadian forces are engaged in hostilities whether or not a state or war exists between Canada and the countries whose forces they are.
Thus it will be treason to assist any armed forces against whom Canadian forces are engaged, whether or not a legal state of war exists between Canada and the country whose forces they are, and whether or not those forces can legally be described, that is in the technical sense, as being enemy forces. Moreover, the amendment removes any doubt that a person may be tried for the offence in Canada, whether or not the offence is committed in Canada.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
The objective of this clause is laudable, but its implications are very dangerous. I should like to find out from the minister what other parts of the commonwealth have brought in a provision such as this. I know of no case in four or five hundred years' interpretation of the law

of treason that goes as far as this amendment. Is there within the British commonwealth or in the United States anything approaching this amendment? I read the discussion that took place by reason of the fact that several persons in this country had gone behind the iron curtain and returned to glorify what they had seen. I have been told of others that have gone to Korea to give comfort to the forces operating against the United Nations. But when the Canadian parliament is asked to pass legislation that makes it treason to assist any public enemy either while in Canada or out of Canada, I should like to ask, however laudable the objective may be, what authority there is for so doing, and whether or not the law officers of the crown have concluded that such a course is lawful.
I can think of an example recently where the authority of the Canadian government did not extend to the making of an order in council legalizing the use of Chinese crews in ships operating under the Canadian ensign in Asiatic waters without having first secured an order in council applicable to Hong Kong. Under this section the Canadian parliament is asked to grant the power to punish for wrongdoing beyond the confines of Canada so far as the crime of treason is concerned. It is for these reasons that I ask that we do not pass an amendment to the Criminal Code that is not within the powers and the jurisdiction of parliament.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
My hon. friend raises two
questions with regard to government policy. First of all, he questions whether we have the power to pass in this parliament an amendment which will apply to an offence which takes place outside of Canada or, to put it in one or two words, whether this parliament has extraterritorial powers. I am sure that if my hon. friend reflects he will remember that when Canada was a colony this parliament did .not have extraterritorial powers, but that following the passage by the British parliament of the Statute of Westminster in 1931 this parliament was placed in possession of extraterritorial powers which have not since been questioned.
My hon. friend asks whether this has been considered by the law officers of the crown. It may be that at common law there is the power to try a case for treason which was committed beyond the confines of the realm and to punish for it if one can secure the offender and try him. Treason within the meaning of the Criminal Code prima facie is under the Criminal Code as it stands at the present time, before this amendment, an offence only if committed inside Canada. The statute as it stands now does not provide
80709-294J
Criminal Code
extraterritorial operations. As I understand my hon. friend, he is objecting to our exercising extraterritorial jurisdiction.

As I was saying, an offence
of treason at common law may be tried by a court notwithstanding that it is committed outside the country in which the court has jurisdiction.

speechtext: That is the Joyce case.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
No; that Joyce case dealt with another point altogether-whether a person who was an alien acquired a certain liability to the United Kingdom at criminal law by reason of the fact that he was operating under a British passport. The case that establishes the point I am referring to now was an even more famous case, the King v. Casement, which was decided in 1917. As hon. members will recall, in that case Sir Roger Casement was charged with high treason alleged to have been committed outside the United Kingdom contrary to the Treason Act of 1351. That was a statute of Edward III which provided, inter alia:
*-if a man do levy war against our lord the king in his realm or be adherent to the king's enemies in his realm, giving to them aid and comfort in the realm or elsewhere ... it is to be understood that in the cases above rehearsed, that ought to be adjudged treason which extends to our lord the king . . .
Chief Justice Reading, at page 123 of 1917, 1 King's Bench report, 98, stated:
I have no hesitation myself in stating that if a man adhere to the king's enemies without the realm he is committing the offence of treason; and that he is committing the offence of treason at common law, notwithstanding that the offence is committed without the realm.
Other members of the court agreed with the chief justice. In the court of appeal it was held unanimously that the statute of Edward III applied and reference was not made to the common law in the appeal court judgment. In the result, therefore, it would appear that at the present time to assist outside of Canada an enemy at war with Canada is an offence at common law, punishable in Canadian courts. It may also be that this statute of Edward III operates in Canada. But the purpose of the present clause of the bill is not what my hon. friend fears, to establish some new invasion of the liberty of the subject. It is to put beyond doubt the position of the common law in Canada and to settle the question whether or not the Canadian parliament, perhaps by reason of the fact that in the Criminal Code it had dealt with this subject, had thereby ousted any effect that the statute of Edward III might still have in this country. We contend that the proposed amendment will

. Criminal Code
remove these doubts. That is the reason we submit it, and we disagree with my hon. friend that it involves any new invasion of the liberty of the subject.
The other point my hon. friend referred to was whether there was any example in the other countries of the British commonwealth of nations of treason being defined as an offence in cases where the armed forces of those parts of the commonwealth were contending against enemy armed forces, but where a state of war did not formally exist between the member of the commonwealth and the nation which had put these armed forces in the field. I-and I am sure I can speak for my staff as well-did not take a poll of what has been done by other members of the commonwealth in this connection, but I should think it is very questionable indeed whether these other countries have taken any such action as we now propose. The reason, I would imagine, for this might be that so far as I am aware we have had before in the history of the commonwealth few if any situations parallel to that which is now occurring in Korea, where, with no declaration of war between the nations whose forces are engaged in the Korean campaign, the soldiers are actually fighting one another. Our view in submitting this clause to the house is that anyone who gives aid and comfort to armed forces with which Canadian forces are in fact engaged in hostilities is in substance just as guilty of treason as if a formal declaration of war had been made and no hostilities were in progress, as was the case during the so-called cold war in the early part of world war II.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: I was seeking information and not taking a stand on this question. I said it was a laudable objective, and I was seeking information; but certainly the Casement case does not help my hon. friend. The Casement case and the reference to the statute of Edward III had to do with enemies with whom the nation was at war. I now ask my hon. friend whether it is the interpretation of the law officers of the crown that what is taking place today in Korea is indeed a state of war with an enemy, although undeclared.

who in fact give comfort to the enemy forces as one making such persons guilty of treason under the code.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.

To have a guilty mind, of course, is, in terms of my hon. friend's question, to begin with a knowing mind. In other words, if the pilot is conducting some person whom he has no reason to suspect of any desire of helping the enemy-

Once you have it, unless there is some misdirection or something of that sort which will result in a quashing of the conviction, there it is, and it justifies itself. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.

The minister may feel that in legalistic terms he has answered the question that is bothering me, but as a layman I would like to put it again since one can always hope to get a layman's answer, even from the minister. What bothers me is the meaning of this word "assisting". The minister keeps using it, and keeps saying that a conviction would depend upon the jury being satisfied that the person charged had actually assisted the enemy. I note that it is the same word that is in the present subsection (i). Is there any place in the code, or in statutory form anywhere, where the meaning of "assistance" is spelled out? Is it confined to overt acts? Can it include the spoken word or the written word? Can it include trading-I am not referring now to the case mentioned by the member for Nanaimo-by any company in Canada, shall we say, with a country some of whose nationals might be engaged in hostilities with Canadian nationals?
I press the point, Mr. Chairman, because it is a rather serious matter with which we are dealing. We are amending a section of the Criminal Code to which is attached the penalty of death, and we should be sure what we are doing is necessary, and that it is being done properly. The only other point I should like to draw attention to is that subsection (i) as it now stands in the Criminal Code, while it is limited to countries actually at war, and by that we mean a state of war being declared, did contain the phrase "assisting any public enemy by any means whatever". I notice that in the revised form the words "by any means whatever" are left out and we are just left with the word "assisting". Will the minister comment on what I have just said?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
My comment would be this. "Assisting" is a word which has been in the Criminal Code for very many years. The only useful answer that might be given to the hon. member would be to refer him to the
[Mr. Garsor.l
cases which have been decided under this section. I do not think there are very many in that time. But I am sure that if he will stop and reflect upon the matter he will realize, whether he be a lawyer or a layman, that the purpose of this word "assisting" in the bill is to describe a certain concept. Now, this particular branch of the crime of treason, that is "assisting the enemy", is one which I suggest to him could take place in a great variety of ways. If the draftsman, instead of using the one word "assist," attempted to specify or spell out all the ways in which assistance could be given to the enemy, he would have a section which would be very much more voluminous than the one before us, and I think less clear and less enforceable. The only question which the jury have to ask themselves on a prosecution under this wording is, did the accused, on the facts which have been brought before us, assist the enemy? To that simple question they could give an answer of acquittal or conviction.	.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.

The great body of Canadians, Mr. Chairman, are laymen, not lawyers or

members of parliament. They know we are at war with China, without any fooling or diplomatic correspondence about the silly thing at all. The diplomats are walking around with eggs in their shoes, because they are afraid they might bring on an allout war; that is the truth of the situation. The people of Canada, not the lawyers but just John Citizen, are wondering how many times we are going to have an undeclared war where our men and women are being killed in defence of this country and our principles. How much longer are we going to ship munitions to a country, whether they are wrapped up in packing cases or cellophane or any other-

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was speaking of the laymen, the great majority of the people in Canada, not the lawyers. I am not sure whether they are fortunate or unfortunate. I am just John Citizen, a member of parliament. I want to know if this is what we need in order to make sure that the only people who can ship to the countries with whom we are at war will be the government. Everyone else will be so afraid they are going to break this particular law that they will not even ship cream puffs. I do not want to see the enemy starve. If we want to send them some wheat, let the government do it. I am afraid when the laymen get into that business and it is not under the direct supervision of the government, grenades will be underneath the wheat that is shipped. I am sorry to say that even natural-born Canadians might be involved in actions of that kind. With the great majority of people, we cannot afford to take a chance.
I am hoping that this section is what we have been trying to get for three wars. I am hoping it will stop shipment of anything out of this country that will be useful to the enemy in killing our men and women. There should not be any pussyfooting on this amendment. It should be quite clear and concise, not stepping all around the situation and saying: Well, if a man does not know that steel can be made into a hand grenade or a 25-pounder, if he cannot prove that in his heart he knew that, if he is just a simpleton, we have to let it go at that, and find that, three weeks later, grenades made of that
Criminal Code
simple bar of steel are being chucked back at our men. That sort of thing must stop. The people of Canada are crying for it.
I only hope that the minister knows what the people of Canada want and that he has, beyond doubt, put the necessary teeth into this amendment so that there may be no more skating on such thin ice, as has been done repeatedly in the past right until there is a declaration of war, right until the enemy stock up enough munitions to come out with a war. Munitions were being continually shipped in the first great war and the second great war, and even now it is going on. I hope that the minister knows what the people of Canada are praying for, and that the teeth are in this amendment beyond any shadow of doubt, to such an extent that no person will dare to do this because he would be afraid he is breaking the law, for fear that he will be put against the wall and have his brains blown out, as he justly deserves to have done. I hope that provision is in this amendment.

It is an extremely serious situation if we are going to continue to allow ships under Canadian registry to be used to repatriate Chinese, as admitted by the Department of Trade and Commerce in the issue of June 16 of Foreign Trade, and to take them back into Canton. Surely something will be done in this regard. I asked the question-and I am sure the hon. member for Nanaimo had the same motive- in an earnest desire to see whether or not the amendments that are being passed really have in them the teeth that the hon. member for

Simcoe North mentioned or are merely window dressing. Here is an opportunity to use them. It seems passing strange that a crew of Chinese, no doubt communists or they would not be getting into Canton, travel on a Canadian ship with a Canadian flag. We can hear them sing: O Canada, we stand on guard for thee.
I say I would like to see this cover cases such as that. In view of the fact that the minister-though he is not supported by the parliamentary assistant to the Secretary of State for External Affairs-and the responsible officer, says, "If we can actually take them in custody, then they are subject to punishment under this act, because they are on a Canadian ship"-then, that being so, when they are in Hong Kong, in a British possession, would it not now be open to the government to stop the things that have been going on and that were brought before the house by the hon. member for Nanaimo?

speechtext: For the simple reason that to answer my hon. friend's question, as my hon. friend who is a lawyer probably knows -it may be that is why he has asked it- one would have to have a good deal of clari* fication as to whether the people he speaks about knew about this, whether they had a guilty mind. As my hon. friend knows-and I am sure he does know-particularly in a charge of treason the guilty mind is of the essence; and unless that is brought home to the accused person it is impossible to establish a conviction. I do not mind answering hypothetical questions within reason, but I must draw the line at that one.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: We say that these people have a guilty mind, and you know what they are doing. Then what?

speechtext: It is up to a jury to decide whether they have a guilty mind or not.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
I would ask the minister to enlighten me as to whether or not this section, in its present form, would be sufficient
Criminal Code
to cover a person who is not assisting the actual armed forces of a country against whose armed forces Canadian forces are engaged in hostilities, but a person who gives general assistance to that country, not specifically related to its armed forces.
I have in mind a case such as that which was reported recently. That was the case of Mrs. Roscoe Rodd, who as someone has just pointed out, come originally from Windsor, Ontario. She broadcast the results of her alleged visit to Korea. Her broadcast material included certain references which were hostile to, and certainly not intended to assist, the cause of the United Nations, of whose forces the Canadian brigade forms a part.
I ask this question because the section is confined to a person who assists any armed forces against whom Canadian forces are engaged in hostilities. It seems to me that a skilful defence counsel might very well raise the defence that such person was not directly assisting the armed forces of that country, but was simply broadcasting an expression of opinion. I should like to know whether this section is sufficient to cover a case such as that, which it seems to me is clearly in broad general terms a case of treason. But, because we are not at war with China or Korea officially or legally, it might be argued that the mere act of broadcasting in favour of China or Korea, which it would be said is not assisting their armed forces, would not be brought within this section.
If the intention of the section is to cover the case of a person giving aid and comfort to the country with whose forces our forces are engaged in hostilities, although we are not legally at war with that country, would the minister say this section is broad enough to cover the case of Mrs. Rodd?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, as I said, I am exceedingly anxious to co-operate as much as I can; but to ask me to prophesy with regard to a set of facts which may be only partially recorded in the newspapers, and then to ask me if that set of facts is covered by the section, is I suggest hardly fair. I would find it exceedingly difficult to do so. My hon. friend is a lawyer, and he is asking me in effect to express a legal opinion upon a set of facts on which he would never dream of expressing a legal opinion.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
No, I am not asking the minister to do that. Perhaps I have not made myself clear. I do not wish to be narrowly technical. I take it the intention of the section is to enable us to deal with persons who go out of Canada and who, if I may use the
4640

Criminal Code
general expression, give aid and comfort to a country which would be described as an enemy, except for the fact that we are not legally at war with it. That is why the original words of this section are being amended.
It seems to me that when reference is made to a person who assists the armed forces of such a country, you may have to prove that the aid or assistance was given directly to the armed forces. Because, as my hon. friend knows without my mentioning it, when you are attempting to prove a charge under the Criminal Code you have to relate the evidence specifically to the intent of the charge.
I am wondering whether it would not be safer if, as I take it, the intention of the section is broadly speaking to cover such treasonable acts, to use some such words as I shall suggest-and in doing so I am not trying to be narrowly technical. I am just trying to cover the general case, because it seems clear to me that Mrs. Rodd was guilty of treason, whether or not she could be found guilty under the present wording of the act.
It does seem to me we would cover a case such as that if we used these words: "Assisting while in or out of Canada any country against whose armed forces Canadian forces are engaged in hostilities." In this way the offence is the assisting of the country, which is a more general term than the armed forces of the country.
That is the proposal I place before the minister. I believe if we are going to make it workable we must make it cover such cases as treasonable activities of the kind indulged in by Mrs. Rodd.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
Perhaps I can answer now, because I believe I understand the question better. As the hon. member for Lake Centre indicated earlier today, the present provision is a great departure; there is no doubt about that. It is designed to deal with a situation which is illustrated by what has happened in Korea, a situation where we may be engaging armed forces the identity of whose country may be somewhat open to question. My hon. friend shakes his head; but I suggest that in the news we get back from Korea, indicating that we are opposed against this branch or that branch of the armed forces, we are not too sure whether they are North Koreans, Chinese or others. And when we are dealing with a situation of that kind, in drafting this legislation we have related it, as my hon. friend correctly points out, to the armed forces; because that is the definite thing with which we can connect the legislation.

For my own part, I would not want to recommend any change in that. I am sure the draftsmen of the statute would not want to change it, because these points my hon. friend has raised were all very carefully considered in the drafting of what I suppose is one of the first examples of this kind of thing to be attempted anywhere. The hon. member for Lake Centre is probably right in his surmise that there is no precedent for what we are attempting to do here.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: It is more than a surmise because I looked over the statutes in England and the United States.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
Then the hon. member is
doubly right. I am sure that he and the hon. member for Kamloops will approve of our having used caution in drafting this section which we think will hold water for what it purports to do.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: I shall not press the minister to give a legal opinion on a hypothetical set of circumstances, but is he able to say whether the officers who drafted this bill had in mind that broadcasts such as those undertaken by Mrs. Rodd or by Joyce would be construed as giving aid or assistance to the armed forces? Is that the assumption on which this section is drawn?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
Will not my hon. friend
agree with me that whether a broadcast was considered as assisting the enemy would depend altogether upon the circumstances under which the broadcast was carried on. If the broadcasting was done from army headquarters in Korea to the armed forces in an effort to incite when translated into their language, it might be one thing. I am always hesitant about tying myself down in connection with a hypothetical case, but I think under those circumstances you might still bring home a charge to the accused although the jury might throw it out. If the broadcasting were done under a different set of circumstances it might not by any conceivable concept of the matter be considered as giving assistance to the armed forces. I think my hon. friend will agree with that statement.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes. That is why I feel that there should be something by way of seeking to make any act of aiding the enemy or hostile country a treasonable offence. We have, for the very reason the minister has given, to make it clear that such assistance is not necessarily confined to direct assistance to the armed forces of a hostile country, but is in fact any act which assists a country against whose forces we are engaged in hostilities, even though a legal state of war may not exist.

The minister put his finger upon the very difficulty I envisaged, and that is that it might well be held by a jury that this type of broadcast did not directly assist the armed forces of that country, yet the broadcast may have been made with the direct intention of assisting the country although it had no relationship necessarily to the armed forces of that country.
I realize that you cannot go too far in one jump, but it seems to me that here we have a section with the clear intent of making it a treasonable offence to assist the country with whose forces Canadian forces are engaged in hostilities, and yet we stop short of expressing the whole offence in proper legal language. We express only a very narrow part of that offence, the part which is perhaps the least likely to take place, that is giving assistance to the armed forces of that country. It seems to me that with the legal language in the section as it stands we have stopped far short of the actual intent which we had in mind when we set out the purport of the section itself.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
There is just one thing in connection with that. I do not think anyone reading that section could ever conclude that it would be an offence under that section to do the things referred to by the hon. member for Kamloops. It would be going a considerable way to make it an offence punishable with death to broadcast unless it directly incited or assisted the enemy. However, as this happened in Canada, I think the sections dealing with sedition would cover it. If any alleged offence has been committed by this woman in broadcasting or if anyone else aroused disaffection to His Majesty and his subjects, it would likely be an offence under the section dealing with sedition, sedition being defined as follows:
Sedition consists in acts, words, or writings intended or calculated, under the circumstances of the time, to disturb the tranquility of the state, by creating ill-will, discontent, disaffection, hatred or contempt towards the person of the King, or towards the constitution or parliament, or the government, or the established institutions of the country, or by exciting ill-will between different classes of the King's subjects, or encouraging any class of them to endeavour to disobey, defy, or subvert the laws or resist their execution, or to do any act of violence or outrage, or endangering the public peace.
If any offence was committed, it would be committed under that section which of course is subject to the following proviso:
133A. No one shall be deemed to have a seditious intention only because he intends in good faith,-
(a)	to show that His Majesty has been misled or mistaken in his measures; or

I am raising this question because this is the high court of Canada in which at this time laws are being made of immense consequence to the people of Canada. For that reason no one need apologize for seeking to clarify in every possible way the legal consequences of the amendment and the explanations given as to precedents. For that reason I would point out

Criminal Code
that there seems to be some misapprehension as to how it was that Joyce was found guilty. In that case the indictment left no doubt that it was necessary to establish that he did owe a positive allegiance to the king. The original indictment read "a person owing allegiance to our lord the king." Then when the question arose as to whether that was a sufficient measure of obligation to the crown the attorney general, representing the crown, indicated that he wanted no doubt as to the measure of obligation that was under consideration, and moved to amend the indictment so that it would read "British subject owing allegiance to our lord the king." In other words this was not simply an American citizen who happened to have the protection of a British passport; it was a British subject. In the arguments before the court it was quite frankly admitted that unless they were prepared to find that he was a British subject their case might fall on that ground alone. The point upon which the court was able to find that he was a British subject and therefore came under the indictment was in these words: that at the time he applied for his passport he made a declaration which used these words:
I, the undersigned, William Joyce, hereby declare that I am a British subject by birth, having been born at Rutledge Terrace, Galway, Ireland, on the 24th day of April, 1906, and not having lost the status of British subject thus acquired, I hereby apply for a passport for travelling.
That was the declaration which, in spite of certain attempts to show that Joyce had acquired citizenship in the United States, was used as the basis for the argument that ultimately led to his being found guilty under the wording in the indictment which I read. I have referred to that for this reason. I hope we shall not be placed in the position of accepting pious declarations as to our intention to deal effectively with activities of the nature contemplated by an amendment of this kind, if in fact the amendment does not do what we want it to do. This is the time to be sure that if we are going to deal with treason of this kind, in other words with these communist traitors, our laws will make it possible to do so effectively. As I understand, the questions were directed to the minister so that this house could have some information as to whether in fact this amendment was more than a general declaration that those who assisted an enemy with whom we were at war, or the armed forces fighting against our forces even though a state of war had not been declared, could in fact be found guilty under the Criminal Code. I would like to know the basis upon which the minister thinks this amendment will be adequate to deal with the sort of case that has
