speechtext:
On a question of privilege just before the minister answers, I am now given to understand that in the question I asked the minister having relation to the case of Mrs. Rodd, I said the broadcast to which I had reference, which I felt should come under this section, was made after her return to Canada, and I gather that this statement gave rise to the question by the hon. member for Spadina. If I said that I was not expressing the thought I had in mind. I do not recollect saying it, and I certainly did not mean to say it. I understood clearly from the press reports to which I had reference that her broadcast was made in Korea, and that it was made while she was in North Korea. It was in reference to an action of that kind that I asked whether that type of broadcast, in a country against whose forces Canadian forces are engaged in hostilities, would come within the ambit of this section, the broadcast not necessarily being of direct assistance to the armed forces of that country but rather of general assistance to the country itself. I have no hesitation in saying that in my opinion a broadcast made in those circumstances comes within the broad general definition of treason and should be within the ambit of this section. That would not apply to a broadcast made after her return to Canada, which as the hon. member for Lake Centre has pointed out would come within the definition of sedition, and I certainly did not mean to refer to any broadcast but the one made in North Korea.
I wanted to clear up that point. My question had reference to the type of broadcast made by Joyce during the war and made by Mrs. Rodd in Korea under circumstances which are not war, because we are not legally at war, but which in effect was designed to aid a country against whose forces Canadian forces are engaged in hostilities.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
The leader of the opposition
has rightly said that this is a matter of considerable importance. He is also quite right in saying that we should do everything we can to make sure that before passing this section the members clearly understand what it means. After all the discussion that has taken place I must confess that I do not

Criminal Code
know of any better way of attempting a further clarification of this section than to start with the law as it stands now, and show the change that has been made by this section; then state what seems to me to be the effect of that section.
Section 74 of the Criminal Code starts out with the words "Treason is", and then,
(a) the act of killing His Majesty, or doing him any bodily harm tending to death or destruction, maim or wounding, and the act of imprisoning or restraining him;
Then there are paragraphs (b), (c), (d), (e), (f) "levying war against His Majesty . . and so on; (g), (h), and then the one we are now amending, paragraph (i) which reads as follows, taking in the first two words of the section:
Treason is,
(i) assisting any public enemy at war with His Majesty in such war by any means whatsoever;
Now, that is the law as it stands at the present time. That law, as I have indicated, being part of the Criminal Code applies, in terms of the Criminal Code and not of the common law or under this statute of Edward III, only where the act is committed within Canada. Now the first thing which our new section does is to provide that the assistance which constitutes the treason can take place either within Canada, as the law now states, or without Canada. Therefore, the section says "assisting", and then adds these words, "assisting, while in or out of Canada, an enemy at war with Canada." That is the first new principle, the new principle of extraterritoriality. Perhaps it is not new, and perhaps it is covered already under the common law or under this statute of Edward III, but at any rate this section removes any doubt that there might be upon that score and makes it clear that if anyone assists the enemy with whom we are at war, whether it is within Canada or out of Canada, he can be prosecuted and convicted under this section.
This clause then goes on to say, "or any armed forces against whom Canadian forces are engaged in hostilities whether or not a state of war exists between Canada and the country whose forces they are." In other words, in order to support a charge of treason under the law as it now stands it would be necessary, as one of the points that had to be proven in the prosecution, to show that Canada was at war with the other country; whereas under this new provision it is not necessary to show that we are at war with any country. We can show merely that our armed forces are engaged in hostilities against the armed forces of some other state, whether there is a condition of war between us or not. Now, that is a very
new departure in principle, because the cases which the leader of the opposition has cited could not have resulted in a conviction on the circumstances of the Korean situation. Sir Roger Casement and William Joyce were both accused of treason where there had been a formal declaration of war between the United Kingdom and the country against whom the United Kingdom was at that time at war.
Those are the two principles which are involved in the bill. I do not know how I can elucidate them any further than I have. I believe part of the confusion has arisen in connection with this discussion from the fact that the leader of the opposition has correctly stated treason is an offence which is a violation of the allegiance which the subject owes to the king. The hon. member is quite right in stating that. I gathered that the point which he was making, in terms of the question previously asked by the member for Nanaimo, was "How could these Chinese alien sailors on a Canadian ship be convicted of treason since they do not owe allegiance to the king of Canada?" It is true that they do not owe allegiance in the sense in which the hon. leader of the opposition uses that word. But the allegiance necessary to support a charge of treason, as I have had occasion to remark in other debates on other occasions, is not only the allegiance which is owed by someone who may have sworn an oath of allegiance to the king, but it is as set out in Crankshaw's "Criminal Code", and which in turn is a quotation from Halsbury's "Laws of England":
The essence of the offence of treason lies in the violation of the allegiance which is owed to the king; and this allegiance is owed, not only by subjects of the king, but also by an alien living in this country, and receiving the protection of its laws, so long as he is a resident here, even if the state to which he belongs is at war with the king.
Even though he may owe allegiance to his state, while he is in this state he owes allegiance to the king, in this context. So that if an alien has lived in this country under the protection of the laws, and the state of which he is a subject invades the territories and the alien assists the invader, which may be within the terms of his own allegiance to his king, the alien is guilty of treason.
As I said before I dislike intensely giving off-the-cuff opinions, but my offhand opinion is that these alien Chinese, who owe no allegiance to the king of Canada, in the narrow sense, yet if they were as aliens upon Canadian territory, namely a ship of Canadian registry flying the Canadian flag, I should think the probabilities would be that, in that capacity, they would owe sufficient allegiance to the Canadian crown

Criminal Code
to support a charge of treason; and therefore, upon a proper set of circumstances being proven against them, they could be convicted of treason under this new section we are considering.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
I suggest a rereading of this - section in order to cover the situation that we are trying to guard against. This section make it an offence,
(1) assisting, while in or out of Canada, any enemy at war with Canada, or any armed forces against whom Canadian forces are engaged in hostilities whether or not a state of war exists between Canada and the country whose forces they are,
In other words, originally the law of treason provided that a person was guilty of that offence if he was guilty of assisting any enemy at war with Canada. Let us take the example mentioned by the hon. member for Kamloops. Somebody leaves Canada, goes over to Korea, broadcasts over there, tells the Koreans and the Chinese communists that they are right, that Canadians know they are right, that Canadians are forced to fight over there, and that the United Nations organization has no business to be there. When that person afterwards returns to Canada, in my submission that person under the law as it is now constituted is guilty of no offence. That person is not guilty of sedition because the only jurisdiction under the law of sedition as it now stands is as to any offence committed within Canada. If that were not so, the offence of treason would be wherever it is committed, under whatever circumstances. I suggest that a slight rewording of this section would cover the situation.
I suggest that it be reworded in this way:
Assisting, while in or out of Canada, any enemy at war with Canada, or any country with which Canadian forces are engaged in hostilities, whether or not a state of war exists between Canada and the country whose forces they are,

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: Any country with whose armed forces Canadian forces are engaged in hostilities.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
Alternative suggestions can be made. But as the section is now worded, assisting an enemy at war with Canada is the offence of treason as it is now constituted.
My hon. friend says he wants to cover a situation of assisting any country that, while not actively at war with Canada, is in direct hostilities with the forces of Canada, whether or not a declaration of war has been made. That is the situation that is to be covered. If that be so, I suggest a couple of changes there would effect the desired result. As it is now, if a person went over to China, or went to Korea and did any act at all to assist Korea other than assisting the armed forces, he would not be guilty of treason. I do not
[Mr. Garson.l
think it was ever intended to limit the offence in that way. The offence that we are now creating is that of assisting any armed forces against whom Canadian forces are engaged in hostilities. That does not cover assisting the nation whose armed forces are engaged in hostilities with Canada.
I point that out most definitely, and I ask the minister to follow those words, because what it means is this. If a person went over to Korea and supplied the government of Korea with assistance, he would not be guilty of treason under the section which parliament is asked to pass. It is only when it is assistance of the armed forces, not of the nation as such. As it now stands, I submit that a person could go over to Korea, get on the radio and do what Lord Haw Haw did, namely, make the most incendiary of speeches, condemn Canada out of hand, as well as the commonwealth and the United Nations, and there would be no offence under that section and he would not be subject to punishment for sedition either because of the position in which the alleged offence was committed. I ask the minister whether he has given consideration to that point. I know how in 1940, again under the exigencies of the moment, we passed the Treachery Act. It was going to be an act that would protect Canada from within. As a matter of fact we rushed it through so fast and in my opinion it had so many loopholes in it that it was never used during the entire period of the war. In this legislation, as it is now drafted, I feel that we are leaving a loophole through which any guilty Canadian could escape by simply saying:	If I had
assisted an enemy at war, I would have been guilty; but because of the fact that I was assisting a country against which Canada is engaged in hostilities by reason of her obligation under the United Nations, I am not guilty of any attempt because I did not assist the armed forces.
To me the situation is most clear, and it was not as I listened to it read and reread. After all, that is the way-out of discussion- that we Anally arrived at a conclusion. We are not trying to prejudice the minister in any way. We are trying to make this something more than merely a delusion. We want to make it a treasonable act for Canadians to use their citizenship in order to go abroad and there to assist the government of Korea or of any other nation with which, in the future, we may not be officially at war as a nation but will be in the position of a punitive agency under the United Nations. We want to deny to Canadians the opportunity to use their citizenship abroad in effect to destroy Canada's efforts in that regard and to endanger human lives, and the opportunity

to say that by reason of the fact that they do not directly assist the enemy they are guilty of no offence. I ask the minister whether he will give consideration to an alteration. As it stands now the crown has to prove that what was done assisted the armed forces, if the offence is committed abroad. If treason is committed with nations with which we are at war, what has to be established is that the assistance was to the enemy at war. But if it is an enemy with which we are not at war, you have to prove that the assistance was of the armed forces and not the enemy as such.

I feel we have almost exhausted the possibilities of this topic as a subject of discussion. I do not know that I can elucidate the matter further than I have attempted to do already.
There is this fact my hon. friends should keep in mind, and that is that we are really not at war in Korea. We are engaged in a police action of the United Nations which we all most devoutly hope will not result in a war, but in the very opposite of a war. As a matter of fact the proceedings this afternoon were opened by a question of the leader of the opposition upon the government's attitude toward a suggestion made by the Russian representative to the United Nations with respect to the possibility of a cease-fire arrangement.
In this clause we have attempted to invoke a new principle growing out of and related to circumstances, not of war but of this police action. The hon. members ask us to give consideration to these matters they have raised. We have given consideration to them, and this section as it stands represents our best judgment. My hon. friends may not agree with us, but we think that in introducing this new principle we have gone quite far, and this is as far as we are inclined to go. It is not an offhanded opinion; it is our carefully considered judgment in the matter.
Let me take one example of the sort of difficulty we may encounter under the suggestions which have been made by hon. members in the opposition, particularly the hon. member for Lake Centre and the hon. member for Kamloops. Supposing some Canadian is engaged in the treasonable activity of smuggling arms in to the armed [Mr. Fulton.l	'
forces, and it is desired to prosecute the traitor. All that would be necessary, under the section as it now stands, would be to prove what happened. The offence would then take place in relation to the armed forces.
But if we had to identify the nation for whom those armed forces were acting, our prosecution might fail; because if we could not identify the nation we could not prove that we were assisting that nation as the enemy to whose armed forces the arms were being run. So we need not suppose for one moment that if we change the wording from what it is now to this other wording we are necessarily making matters easier. We may make them much more embarrassing for effectual enforcement of this clause.
The fact we are faced with in Korea is this, not that we are at war, but that in the course of police action which we are taking as part of the United Nations forces in that country we are faced with soldiers on the other side fighting us. We have drafted a section under which that is the only thing of which we have to take cognizance. Any assistance given to these soldiers is an offence.
There has been a great deal of discussion at one time or another as to whether there should or should not be normal trade-I do not mean trade in critical materials or materials of war-carried on between Canada and these other countries. There is a large body of responsible and sincere opinion in the United Kingdom and other nations of the United Nations which feels that ordinary peaceful trade should be carried on. If we adopted the language advocated by the hon. member for Kamloops I think he will be the first to admit that you would immediately create a condition of affairs under which it would be extremely difficult, if not impossible, to give effect to that body of opinion. I want to emphasize that I am not saying that that opinion is right or wrong, but what we have attempted to do in the Department of Justice is to draft a clause which would invoke a new principle in such a way that we could make it effective in a practical manner without creating a lot of embarrassment to the policies of the United Nations.
We think that after giving consideration to all these matters which have been raised by members of the opposition and others- we were able to give it longer attention than has been possible this afternoon-this wording represents our best judgment as to the most effective manner of dealing with the question.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not propose to extend this argument simply for the purpose of extending the debate on this section. When the minister raises the point that it might be difficult to obtain a conviction under such amendment in whatever actual wording it might be interpreted, I would point out how difficult it is going to be to obtain a conviction under this section as now drafted. I do not like passing an amendment simply as a gesture if I do not think it is going to produce some results. This strikes out the old subsection of the section in the Criminal Code dealing with the various definitions of treason. It strikes out paragraph (i) of subsection 1 of section 74, and the words it strikes out are, "assisting any public enemy at war with His Majesty in such war by any means whatsoever." In this case the suggested amendment, after striking out those words, would provide that it was an offence to assist, while in or out of Canada, any enemy at war with Canada. So far that is the same as the old section even if there is a slight change in that it provides "in or out of Canada." In that respect I repeat the observation I have made as to the difficulty of extending the law unless they are Canadian citizens or British subjects, but we will leave that for the moment.
It then goes on to the second thing that is regarded as important and that is the situation that the Minister of Justice has described as new, where forces sent from Canada along with forces from other countries are actively engaged in a deadly war with an enemy supplied by a nation against whom there has been no declaration of war. An attempt is made to provide an offence where there is assistance to those undeclared enemies. The way that the amendment would do it is to provide that it is an attempt to assist any armed forces against whom Canadian forces are engaged in hostilities.

May I point out that the proof would be almost an impossibility. How are you going to prove it is helping the enemy forces? Are you going to take an officer you have captured and have him swear that he was assisted in a certain battle by supplies he got? Are you going to be able to call into the witness box people from the enemy forces and have them declare that a broadcast was of assistance to those forces? How are you going to prove it? Surely it would not be acceptable evidence for someone on our side to say that they thought that the enemy must have obtained some benefit from the broadcast,	weapons or supplies which
reached it.
I do not think it is possible to prove, except in the most unlikely case, that assistance actually reached the armed forces, but it is easy enough in many cases to prove that assistance reached the nation from which those armed forces come. So far as I am concerned, I think we should stop pussyfooting. We are at war with China under its present government. We may not be in a declared war but this war as it stands at the present time is a war that has already killed more men than were killed in the whole Pacific war in the first year after Pearl Harbor. It is true that it is not a declared war, but let us, without suggesting that it is necessary for us to declare a war, admit that, while we seek peace with China on terms that are honourable and that will lay a foundation for peace, we also recognize the fact that from their statements in conferences they have attended, from the broadcasts that have been received by our monitors, the government of China is not only accepting responsibility for the Chinese troops in Korea but is boasting to their own people what those troops are doing.
Therefore we know perfectly well that the nation that is supplying the troops against whom our troops are fighting is communist China, not the people of China but the China of today under a communist government, just as we were dealing a few years ago with the Germany of Hitler although we thought that there were many decent Germans, and just as we were dealing with the Italy of Mussolini although we thought there were many decent Italians. We must deal with the nation as it is, and we are dealing with a nation under a government which boasts of the achievements of its armed men in Korea. I think the time has come when, far from seeking to define our enemies in a way that we shall not give offence to those who might trade with them, we should say we want laws that will make it impossible to trade with those people until we have established a basis of

peace, and that we do not want an amendment which we simply cannot possibly hope to enforce on the basis of any evidence available.
I do not want to reduce this matter to a basis any less serious than it really is, but as I was looking at some figures with respect to the war in Korea I could not help noticing an advertisement with the words, "What might the Mings have done with Alcoa aluminum?" That happens to be a by-product of certain aluminum products. Obviously this is not referring to the Ming Sung company but there are certain Mings connected with it who can do a great deal with aluminum if they see fit. They are doing a lot of things with other products that undoubtedly in some way are assisting those against whom we are fighting at the present time.
The minister has left the impression this afternoon that in certain cases this amendment might make it possible to deal with those who are operating these ships under Canadian registry if in fact it could be proved that the things they were delivering were of assistance to our enemies. I submit that under this amendment they could not because they are carrying the things such as they are carrying to Canton, to a great seaport of the nation which provides the troops, but there is no suggestion they are carrying these things to the seaports along the Korean coast. Yet unless we had people who could go there, see what was taking place and give evidence in a court that they had actually seen the delivery of these things to the men against whom we are fighting, this section would be absolutely ineffective. Unless the Minister of Justice, in whatever words he sees fit, is prepared to go so far as to make it an offence to deliver to the nation from which the armed forces are provided who are fighting against our troops without a declaration of war, then I submit this section can have no value whatever, and I do not think we should be called upon to pass it.

I will interrupt my remarks to answer my hon. friend and tell him that while Truman says "the United States is ready to talk peace but it must be real", according to the five o'clock edition of the newspapers, he does not say we are at war with China. If my hon. friend will be patient and let me finish my argument I am sure he will agree with me. In the first place he will agree that in virtue of the modern international law, not as it is taught in universities but as it is practised in this world, Canada is not at war with anybody. We were at war during the first and second world wars. We were at war during the South African war. We were at war with the Indians in the first days of the colony. At the present time we are at war with no one though our soldiers go there with guns and ammunition and shoot the Chinese and others. We are just policing the world for the United Nations, and this must be taken into account in drafting our law, because our law must apply not to the past but to the present and future. My hon. friend will admit that. What is the use of adopting legislation that is inoperative and

Criminal Code
will serve only for academic discussion? My hon. friend mentions war and says we are at war with China. If that is the case the legislation cannot operate because in theory we are not. I admit it is a very strange situation, but we must take it as it is.
Therefore very seriously I suggest to the minister that he add something concerning policing and resistance to the policing of any country by the United Nations. The minister, who is a learned jurist and who has had experience as minister for quite a long time, must realize the value of that argument. You cannot catch a bear with a mouse trap. I submit the matter to him. I do not insist, since we are about to end the session, but this is a serious matter which deserves the consideration of everyone, the Department of Justice as well as the opposition. Now I challenge the expert jurists of the opposition group; I will ask my genial friend from Lake Centre in all honesty to tell us if we are officially at war with any country now. To be at war we must have made a declaration of war. There is none. We are just trying to improve the morals of the Asiatics by sending men with munitions of war to police them. Instead of using the big stick we see in the hands of the constables of any municipal police force or the stick that adorns the uniform of the constables of the House of Commons, our soldiers go there with rifles and bullets and bayonets. They act just the same as though they were at war, but they are not at war juridically, and my hon. friend will admit that they are not at war.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
This section amends the old
one which dealt with desertion. It now reads:
Everyone who aids, assists, harbours or conceals a person whom he knows is a deserter or an absentee without leave from the Canadian forces is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding five hundred dollars.
I wish the minister would give us some reason for including the words "or an absentee without leave". After all, as I understand it, qne only has to be a.w.o.l. for twenty-eight days when he becomes a deserter. Can you imagine any parent whose boy came home without leave not assisting him? I cannot understand why such a parent would have to be classed as a criminal and fined $500. I personally feel that the section should be left to deal with deserters only. If it does deal with persons absent without leave the words "aid and assist" should be left out. I would ask the minister to give us some explanation concerning this.
I would suggest that the words "absent without leave" be deleted or at any rate if they must remain for any good reason, certainly no prosecution should be instituted under this section except upon the representations of the attorney general of the province. I have an example in mind which occurred a few months ago. A lad came home on Christmas leave, and immediately after Christmas his mother had a heart attack. She lingered for ten or fourteen days and then died. By staying with his mother the young lad was a.w.o.l., but he was not a deserter. Under this section his father was liable to a fine because he aided and assisted a person who was absent without leave. I am suggesting that a person only has to be absent without leave for twenty-eight days- at least that used to be the case-when he automatically becomes a deserter. I think that section should be amended and the words "absent without leave" be deleted. At any rate some safeguard should be put in there, so that a prosecution could not be instituted by some neighbour who wished to cause trouble for some parent who aided a boy who came home and overstayed his leave.

remarks rather impressive with regard to the absent without leave, and I can imagine a set of circumstances under which some spite work might be done. I would be willing to recommend to the committee that, where necessary, the Attorney General of Canada should be written into the act, if
Criminal Code
that would be all right. I think we shall draft a provision and have it moved after the dinner adjournment. Let the clause stand.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: There is all the difference in the world between absent without leave and desertion, because in desertion you have to prove the intent to desert whereas absence without leave might be due to accident or something of that sort. There is one other point I should like to make in connection with this section; should it not apply to a deserter from allied forces? I ask that question because we might have allied forces operating in Canada, and a deserter from those forces might be harboured by a Canadian citizen. It seems to me that there should be some clause to cover that point also.

speechtext: May I ask the minister how this works out with regard to boys who are coming home and who are carrying souvenirs? How does this provision work?

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
When they come home carrying souvenirs which are pistols or revolvers, they will have to comply with the act by registering them and getting the usual permit to have them. The man who has two or three

Criminal Code
pistols or revolvers like that gets those permits and carries them. I have known of several who have done that. As a matter of fact, if that provision were not made, it would be difficult to keep track of all the pistols and revolvers in the country. The purpose of this section is to do just that.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: I am not kicking against the registration. What I am saying is that these boys pick up these revolvers and pistols and bring them home to this country as souvenirs. They keep them on them. They do not know anything about this act. It is a change. How are those boys going to be notified that when they bring these over they can be prosecuted and fined? They do not know anything about it.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: I am afraid that the old saw that ignorance of the law excuses no person happens to be a correct statement of the situation.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: But in most cases a situation of that kind is covered by a little bit of discretion exercised either by the crown prosecutor, the police or the magistrate taking into consideration the fact that the accused appears to be quite innocent in not having known about these provisions. The point that my hon. friend is referring to applies of course to every law on the statute books in the country.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: Not every person knows of the existence of these laws, but they are there; and it is necessary to have the principle that people are supposed to know the law. Otherwise they would always have the excuse for breaking the law that they did not know it was the law.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.

speechtext: Would it not be contrary to the military regulations for any private individual to take enemy arms? They are all supposed to be turned in.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
That is what a general would say. He says that they are not supposed to take them; but they take them and the general winks at it. Section 120 in section 7 of the bill prohibits anybody from using a

twenty-two or an air rifle up to the age of 14. I should like the minister to have that age reduced down to 12 for the simple reason that there are many boys who learn to shoot, to run tractors and everything else, and who carry these twenty-two rifles all the time for the purpose of shooting gophers. As for myself, at 13 I could shoot better than I can now.
There may be something to be said for what these fellows are talking about as far as they are concerned. But as far as western Canada is concerned, it is ridiculous. There is no doubt about that. Take the case of a young fellow who prides himself on having a twenty-two. If he is a young fellow 13 years of age, he has got to get rid of it.' Yet he goes out and shoots gophers, and does a job that is worth while. In the far north there are many occasions when a boy going to school must carry a twenty-two in order to protect himself. Why should the age be set at 14? Somebody has a bug in his ear that should be taken out.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.

speechtext: All I can say is that it is a provision which has been honoured more in the breach than in the observance. I think most boys on our farms-in the west, at any rate-have had twenty-two rifles, and sometimes larger ones, many years before the age of 14. It seems to me to be a rather bad provision to make it a crime to give a gun to a boy who was brought up on a farm, and where people have been accustomed to shooting gophers from the age of 9 or 10, in some cases. I see no real purpose to be served by this section. I wonder if the minister could tell us what real purpose is to be served by it?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: I must say that I am not an expert in this field but I should have thought that this proposed section, and the present section 126, since they apply to the whole of Canada-to both rural and urban parts-have been produced perhaps because in the cities and in the suburbs of the cities, some difficulty has arisen through the abuse of twenty-two rifles, by boys of that age. This abuse may have come to the attention of members of the chief constables association; and may have made them think that it is undesirable that boys under fourteen in their observation and experience, should have possession of a twenty-two rifle. I think my hon. friend will agree that there is some difference between a rural boy who has objects in nature to shoot at and the urban boy who has not, as to the situation that possession of a twenty-two rifle might create in one case as compared with the other. I think that the needs of both hon. members would be met by retaining the permit system from 14 years of age down. It is not a matter which I, as Minister of Justice, can take any cognizance of but I am inclined to agree with my hon. friend that this provision sometimes has been more honoured in the breach than in the observance.

Every one is guilty of an offence who has an unregistered firearm in his dwelling house or place of business.

We will pass that one. There is provision for registration. I should like to draw the minister's attention to subsection 2. It reads:
Every one is guilty of an offence who has a firearm elsewhere than in his dwelling house or place of business, unless he has a valid permit in Form 76 or Form 76B	
Form 76B provides for transportation of a firearm. With reference to form 76, if the minister will look at section 125, subsection 4, he will find you can only get that permit if you certify that you need the firearm to protect your life, in connection with your profession, or for use in target practice at a range which has been approved by the attorney general of the province. The matter I should like to bring to the minister's attention is this. Rightly or wrongly the definition of firearm includes-we are dealing now with the specialized definition-[DOT] a revolver or pistol or automatic rifle. Rightly or wrongly many people, at least in eastern Canada, use automatic rifles when they go hunting. Whether or not they should' is perhaps a question of sportsmanship. It certainly does not affect the legality of it. This is the position in whidh you find yourself under this section. A man has to get a permit to take his rifle away from his own residence, and he can only obtain it if he certifies that he needs it to protect his life, for use in his profession or for use at a target range. Therefore he can never obtain a permit to take the rifle out in the woods when he goes hunting.
I am sure that was not the intention of the draftsmen of the section, and it is something which I think should receive the attention of the department. I am simply bringing it to the minister's attention. Personally I have not very much sympathy with people who go hunting with automatic rifles, but they are probably just as good citizens as I am, and I know they use them. It is impossible under the wording of the section to get a permit to take it away from your home into the woods. I draw that to the minister's attention and suggest that he give it some consideration.
Then I cannot understand subsection 3 which says that everyone who is an occupant of a motor vehicle in which he knows there is a firearm is guilty of an offence unless some occupant has a certificate. With all deference, I suggest that is more reminiscent of the liquor acts and the bootlegging acts of twenty years ago. I may drive along the road with a rifle in my car, a firearm, and I pick up someone and take him along. I have not had the firearm registered. The person I may have picked up-it might be the minister or it might be my wife whom

I am taking for a drive or anyone else-is liable to be convicted of an offence because the firearm is there without proper registration. It seems to me that the section goes further than was ever intended by the minister, and I should like to have his comments.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
That section has been in the
law for many years. There is nothing new in this section at all.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: I am sure there is. I do not want to enter into a discussion with the minister. The other section dealt with a revolver or pistol, which is an entirely different thing. I can quite understand why a revolver or pistol, a hidden or concealed weapon, is something to which the most stringent regulations must apply, although frankly I think the minister will admit they were not always effective. Now you are dealing with a rifle, a firearm, and it is an entirely different set-up from a hidden weapon. The minister is not correct when he says there is nothing new because the definition is new.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: My hon. friend's point really is that he objects to the result which is obtained by providing a new definition of firearm to include automatic rifle.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: And by that act bringing the automatic rifle into this provision to which he has now referred.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: That is right.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: We could give that some thought. Might I ask my hon. friend a question? Is not .the automatic rifle barred by the game laws of his province?

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: I do not know. I have never used one myself, but I know many who do use them, and I doubt if they are barred. I know they are used in Nova Scotia.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: I think my hon. friend will find they are barred unless they can satisfy the game wardens that they are adjusted in such a way that they can only fire a limited number of shots.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
Of course I am assuming an automatic rifle is what is intended by that definition. It says one that fires a number of bullets at one pressure of the trigger. However, I know that they are used in Nova Scotia and I know that they have a very efficient game warden service there. Therefore I cannot believe they are illegal if they can be used. Certainly they never can be used under this section.
Criminal Code

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: This provision was put in at the request of the chief constables association because they now regard these automatic rifles as much more dangerous weapons, for obvious reasons, than either pistols or revolvers. Of course what they have in mind chiefly are conditions in the large metropolitan cities where they are not used for the purpose of hunting game.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: I think the minister will admit that all these regulations are honoured more in the breach than in the observance. We are trying to guard the public against the use of dangerous weapons. I think the minister will find that every murder that has been committed with a revolver was with a revolver that had never been registered. What I am objecting to-and I am sure the minister objects to it-is making involuntarily a large class of lawbreakers by prescribing certain statutory regulations which will not be followed.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: I do not think I would entirely agree because we have checked this on another occasion, and there are not such a large number of lawbreakers as my hon. friend might think. It is true the chaps who use these firearms for the purpose of committing crimes are breaking the law, and that they usually have not registered the firearms, but that is the least of their offences against the law.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
I should like to be perfectly
clear about section 127 of this clause. I should like to get an assurance from the minister that this search and seizure provision can apply only to arms, that this section deals altogether with firearms.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: Yes, that is right.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
It seems to me that this is a
pretty wide power when one can enter without a warrant. If there was a warrant then the people would know why the peace officer was searching because he would produce his warrant and it would so stipulate. However, if there is no warrant and no stipulation as to the reason why the search is made, people are liable to be suspicious that the peace officer may be after something else. Is there anything to hinder a peace officer going in with the excuse of looking for firearms when he is really after something else? It looks like an interference with the liberty of the individual.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
I think if my hon. friend will read the language of the section he will see

Criminal Code
that perhaps it is not as far-reaching as he may suspect. The section reads:
Whenever a peace officer believes on reasonable grounds that an offence is being committed or has been committed against any of the provisions of sections 115 to 123-
It is confined to those sections. The fact that the peace officer is proceeding without any warrant to back him up and is acting on his own responsibility, so that if he takes an action which is not upon reasonable grounds he is in for a great deal of trouble himself, I think in most cases would be a very effective deterrent to any abuse of this section. Actually I think you will find in practice that where an officer is clothed with power of this sort, which leaves it on his shoulders to decide whether the grounds are reasonable, he will be very cautious indeed in reaching an opinion as to whether the grounds are reasonable, and perhaps will not act under the authority granted by this section even in cases where he might be able to get authority in the form of a warrant from a magistrate.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
I want to draw the minister's attention to one more matter and then I am through. Section 122 (6) provides:
Everyone who buys or accepts in barter or as a gift a firearm is guilty of an offence if he receives delivery of it-
What happens, for instance, if a man dies and his rifle devolves to his son? It is really a gift; it may be a testamentary one. I am raising this as a serious matter because I am sure the minister, like the rest of us, wants to avoid making statutory criminals out of a lot of people and thereby perhaps creating more and more disrespect for the law. I think there is a weakness in that section which I would like the minister to look at anyway, and see if it can be overcome.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
I would not agree that it really was a weakness, because the clause goes on to say "before it is registered in his name." The purpose here is the very obvious one of making certain that before John Doe takes over that firearm he has it registered in his name. In the case to which my hon. friend refers where the revolver, we will say, devolves to the son, all he has to do is say to the administrators or executors of the estate that he will not take delivery of it until they have it registered in his name. I think that provision is reasonable enough and necessary when we are dealing with instruments which are not only deadly weapons in themselves but which are used in the great majority of the crimes of violence that take place throughout the country. Apart from the question of the registration of firearms by respectable people, it is very much in the

interests of everyone that the strictest sort of provision be made regarding the registration of firearms generally.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: Far be it from me to quarrel with what the minister says about revolvers and pistols, but I am suggesting he has extended the definition to include rifles, at least automatic rifles. I know very well that many people in rural communities-I am certain of this in the east-in the first place will not know the law, and in the second place will not bother registering their rifles, so we will have a large class of involuntary lawbreakers, which is something we should avoid if we are to maintain proper respect for the law. I know the minister would like to get this bill through tonight, and I am not going to hold it up; but I would hope he might give some consideration to this point and provide for a difference between revolvers and pistols on the one hand and rifles on the other, so we will not have a large number of people breaking the law without knowing it. In many of these estates there are no executors; the son just takes over. What do you do in a case like that?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: I wonder if we could not meet my hon. friend's views in this way. The kind of firearm the chief constables association had in mind in this instance was what I believe is known in the trade as a typewriter or submachine gun. It may be that the definition we have put in here will include the type of automatic rifle to which my hon. friend has reference. I suggest that we pass this section and we will discuss the matter with the police. If they are satisfied to have a new wording which, would have the effect of exempting the automatic rifles to which my hon. friend refers, we could make that change in the Senate.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: That would be quite satisfactory to me.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
I am not quite satisfied with the reply the minister gave the hon. member for Saskatoon with regard to the provisions of section 127, which reads:
Whenever a peace officer believes on reasonable grounds that an offence is being committed or has been committed-
How will it be decided that he did not have reasonable grounds? Suppose I am stopped on the street and searched by a policeman without a search warrant, and nothing is found. Where do I get my redress for what has happened? The sanctity of my person, or whatever the term may be, has been violated. Will it be up to me then to take action against the police officer; and where would the ordinary individual be in those circumstances?

Criminal Code

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: Suppose my hon. friend is with friends at a hunting lodge shooting ducks, we will say, at a time when deer are out of season, and some officious minion of the law comes along and makes a general nuisance of himself searching all through the premises with no reasonable grounds for doing so. Perhaps he is searching for the kind of automatic rifle to which the hon. member for Annapolis-Kings referred a moment ago. I should think my hon. friend's first reaction would be to call up the game department of that province and raise a considerable amount of Cain about the sort of game wardens they employed. If in the course of this trespass-because that is what it would be if the officer did not have reasonable grounds-he committed an assault, an information could be laid against him on both those grounds. Then you would have the law enforcer up before the magistrate. Most of these officials are responsible. If before a man acts in a given case he has to decide whether he has reasonable grounds, he is not going to take that responsibility upon his own shoulders unless he is pretty sure the people into whose premises he is going have a prohibited firearm on the premises, or unless he feels that he can show his own superior officers or a magistrate that he actually had reasonable grounds for the action he took.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: But would it not be largely a matter of taking his word against mine? Generally speaking I suppose peace officers act fairly decently, but every now and then we hear of judges complaining that police officers have gone beyond their jurisdiction. I think the ordinary individual would want to know who was to pay for any action he was to take. He would hesitate, and would accept interference with his person and property rather than take action when the cards are stacked against him and it is his word against that of a peace officer. I think this section goes altogether too far.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 8-Miscellaneous offences of a seditious nature.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
With all deference to my hon. friend, I was just asking my assistant to turn up the section of the code which would cover that. I think this is it:
Every one who, having an intent to commit an offence, does or omits an act for the purpose of accomplishing his object-

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: What section is that?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
Section 72. This is a general section, applying not only to this provision but to all offences under the act.
Every one who, having an intent to commit an offence, does or omits an act for the purpose of accomplishing his object is guilty of an attempt to commit the offence intended whether under the circumstances it was possible to commit such offence or not.
That is to say, not only is he guilty-

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: There is no question about it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: May I ask the minister a question that comes at the problem from a little different angle? What protection is there for a person who by his utterances or opinions might have the effect, even unknown to him, of influencing some of these people to lessen their loyalty?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
If the hon. member looks at the last few words of the section:
Every one is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to imprisonment for five years who wilfully...
The case my hon. friend is speaking about concerns one who unintentionally says something which has that effect. He would not be guilty.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
To quote again the kind of concrete example I was quoting this afternoon, and I know of no better example to take than the Secretary of State for External Affairs, supposing he, by the kind of forthright and excellent statement he has been

Criminal Code
making to the effect we cannot defeat communism by military means, has the effect of causing some of these people to cool off in their loyalty towards their military tasks, what protection would he have?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: He does not do what he does with the will to interfere with or impair the loyalty to the forces or the mounted police. If that is purely a consequential result, and he does not have that as his own objective, then he is not guilty under the section. It is only when anyone makes a speech or has a writing or importunes or interferes or impairs the loyalty by acts which are designed for that purpose, and practically no other, that an offence is committed under this section.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
I really want to be sure of that, and I think all of us want to be sure, because the references here are sweeping. The references are to publishing, issuing, editing or ciroulating any writing and so on. Then there are these other words, advising, counselling, urging, etc. I take it that we can count on the fact that section 133A, which is now in the Criminal Code, would have a bearing on the kind of case I was talking about. For example, section 133A, which is just two sections farther down from this one, reads:
No one shall be deemed to have a seditious intention only because he intends in good faith,-
(a)	to show that His Majesty has been misled or mistaken in his measures; or
(b)	to point out errors or defects in the government or constitution of the United Kingdom, or of any part of it, or of Canada or any province thereof, or in either house of parliament of the United Kingdom or of Canada, or in any legislature, or in the administration of justice; or to excite His Majesty's subjects to attempt to procure, by lawful means, the alteration of any matter in the state; or,
(c)	to point out, in order to their removal, matters which are producing feelings of hatred and ill-will between different classes of His Majesty's subjects.
I take it that those two sections will have to be read together, and that there is no question about the right of free speech in relation to matters of criticism of public policy, criticism of the government, and all the things that are traditional so long as the purpose is not as set out in this new section 132A.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: With great deference I think the word "wilfully" in this section, apart altogether from section 133A to which my hon. friend referred, protects any person who has been indulging in discussion in good faith and not with the express purpose of trying to affect the loyalty of these persons or the mounted police.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: It is true, is it not, that this is a new section? We have not had anything like it before in our Canadian Criminal Code.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: That is right.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: I take it that the minister, as a Liberal, has looked at it from the liberal standpoint to which I have been giving expression tonight?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: Correct,

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 9-Punishment for seditious words, seditious libel, seditious conspiracy.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: This concerns the mere increase in the penalty. It is not so much the degree of the penalty as the enforcement that counts. Will the minister state how many convictions there have been under section 134 since 1935?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: I am afraid I could not give my hon. friend the exact number. It would not be large. I believe that in the case of some of the revelations arising out of the Gouzenko affair some charges were laid under this section. Some were laid under the Official Secrets Act. This penalty we have provided here of seven years is the same penalty that is provided under the Official Secrets Act. As my hon. friend knows it may be possible, under a given set of facts, for the crown to choose whether it will lay a charge under one act or the other, and in some cases a charge under each act may be laid. Under the present circumstances we thought that a penalty of two years for the crime of sedition was altogether inadequate, and that it should be raised to equality with the penalty under the Official Secrets Act.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: I think that in increasing the sentence from two years to seven years is a tremendous increase in the penalty for this crime. I appreciate that we are living in dangerous times, and we have to contend with people who have loyalty to another government in another country rather than our own. But surely if we have to adopt the suppressive laws of dictatorship to preserve democracy, then we have lost democracy. I believe that sometimes the words that are considered seditious are a bit flimsy and if a conviction were registered there would be a penalty of seven years instead of the two years. We should always bear in mind that convictions or actions under these sections are liable to be undertaken at times when the minds of people are disturbed, when we are living on the verge of hysteria. I think it is dangerous indeed to make this amendment to this section at the present time. I am not a lawyer and I am not accustomed to speaking in these terms on matters of this kind. But I think we are embarking on really dangerous ground.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
X should like to offer one or two comments in connection with my hon. friend's observations. In the first place, I am sure he realizes that this is the maximum sentence. The judge or the magistrate can impose any lesser sentence that he wishes to impose. His judgment as to sentence is subject to appeal. Then the accused or the convicted person has the right to apply for pardon or for remission of a portion of the sentence.
In addition to that, would my hon. friend not agree that what we are really measuring here is that period of sentence which, under the conditions of today, is the proper maximum sentence? I should think that, under present conditions-which are greatly different from what they were, say, two or three years ago before we were engaged in hostilities although not in war-the crime of sedition is a much more serious one than it was then; and that it is easy enough to imagine a set of circumstances in which the crime of sedition would be serious enough to warrant a sentence of seven years. From that it does not follow by any means that all of the sentences under this section are going to be seven years. One might be for six months; another might be for seven months; another might be for two months; or sentence might be suspended. But where the circumstances are extremely heinous, the magistrate or the judge is given discretion to give a sentence up to seven years.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: The provision for a sentence of not more than two years was in the old section; and the same conditions apply to that term as the minister now applies to the term of seven years. My mind goes back to the conditions prevailing in this country during and shortly after world war I, and to the conditions prevailing in the United States during the same period, when some of the most vicious sentences were imposed for trivial matters. I say again that we are losing out in our way of life when we increase the penalties for crimes that have been in our Criminal Code from time immemorial.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
There are a few comments
that I should like to make. First, I should be interested in any remarks the minister might care to make on the fact that the section we just passed a moment ago, namely section 132A, seemed to spell out, once we got the full definition of that word "wilfully", fairly serious offences. Yet under section 132A, the imprisonment was set at five years. Section 134 seems to be not quite as serious-although maybe I am wrong; I should like the minister to explain it-and yet the penalty can be higher. It can be seven years.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
Is not the answer to that
question a fairly obvious one? Although there are perhaps a number of cases of sedition where the offence on the facts would not be perhaps as serious as an offence under 132A, one can imagine cases of sedition which would be so serious that they would greatly transcend anything that could be done under section 132A.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
In that connection may I
point out that section 133 defines seditious words, seditious intentions, and so on and subsection 4 of section 133 of the code reads as follows:
Without limiting the generality of the meaning of the expression "seditious intention," everyone shall be presumed to have a seditious intention who publishes, or circulates any writing, printing or document in which it is advocated, or who teaches or advocates, the use, without the authority of law, of force, as a means of accomplishing any governmental change within Canada.
Can the minister tell me whether there have been any cases in recent years where charges of sedition have been for offences less serious than that which is spelled out in that section, or has that come to be more or less the common definition of seditious intention, despite the phrase which says that the definition is not limited thereto?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
The word "sedition" will
include everything from the utterances of Jehovah's Witnesses to the utterances upon which Mr. Tim Buck was convicted back in the 1930's. One of the charges against him was that of sedition. The reason why there is this range of penalty, which we think is proper under present conditions, is that it is one thing to commit the offence of sedition in the piping times of peace when sedition can be indulged in without any grave danger to the country, and it is an altogether different thing to commit the offence of sedition at the present time; and it would be even more serious if it were committed during war itself. For that reason we justify the provision that we have here, and the difference between the penalty under section 132A and the one under this present section.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: I want to thank the minister for the inclusion of this provision in the Criminal Code. I hope that it will have the effect of suppressing communist propaganda.

speechtext:
Now that most people
are supposed to have undying loyalty and adoration for the United Nations, rather than Canada, and a wide variety of new outgrowths of imaginings a while ago, I wonder whether or not we are going to have a detailed list of definitions of sedition. I cannot figure out just how a person would know when he was seditious.

speechtext:
I do not know whether it
will reassure my hon. friend if I tell him that the commission we have consolidating the Criminal Code is at present engaged in what is regarded by draftsmen as a quite ambitious undertaking, namely that of defining sedition in terms of what sedition is under the common law. We are expecting them to report fairly shortly. We are going to get that report some time before we thought it would be available, because we have made better progress than we thought we would. When that comes to hand we will be laying it before hon. members.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
I think the point raised by the hon. member for Lethbridge is quite pertinent, because I do not think there is any particular definition of what words are seditious. I remember that a person who later became a member of this house was arrested for publishing seditious libel or making seditious utterances, and one of the charges against him was in respect of several passages from the book of Isaiah. Some of the other passages were from the program of the British Labour party.
The point is that when people become hysterical they will not stop at anything. It is too bad that we have in the law provisions which give them opportunity for discharging duties when they are in an hysterical condition, and when their actions are not based upon law or motivated by law, but based upon and motivated by fear, such as was the case at that time. Any improvement that has come in the lives of the common people has come by the removal of these laws, rather than the multiplication of them.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
We see examples of
things that might give a person cause for wonder, in what is occurring in Canada. I do not recall that ever in this House of Commons, or anywhere else in public where the people's representatives have been assembled, there has been a discussion of the advisability of eliminating the word "dominion" from the name of this nation. The Dominion of Canada is what I was taught to revere, but for some reason or other the word "dominion" is now being left out. There seems to be a movement afoot to make it a sort of faux pas for a person to refer to the "Dominion of Canada"; he is supposed to refer to "Canada".
No one knows how all this has happened, or at whose instance. If things like that are going on, apparently through some sort of ministerial or governmental decree, rather than by an expression of will by the representatives of the people, and if a somewhat

analogous situation develops in respect of this wonderful new United Nations, or the British commonwealth, or the British empire, then I can see the time is coming when people will be at their wit's end to know when they are doing that which is appropriate.
I hope this list of definitions of sedition will be comprehensive and widely publicized. I hope it will be made readily available to everyone who might be in danger of committing an offence against the law of sedition.

of the progress being made by the commission revising the code; but it strikes me as strange that when that commission is engaged on this task, a task which at least in part is parallel to the task embodied in the bill before us, apparently there has not been consultation with the commission in regard to the extensive amendments contained in the bill.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
I think perhaps I can explain it to my hon. friend by drawing this distinction: as he knows, the code has not been overhauled, actually, since 1892. In the interval of time which has elapsed since then, the substance of it, consisting of a lot of changes which have been made from time to time and without too much consideration for reconciling them in terms of one another, has got pretty much involved. The task to which we have set the Criminal Code revision commission is that of revising and consolidating the form of the code, as distinguished from its substance. These amendments which we are bringing down to the

house from year to year, such as the present group of amendments, are the ones in which we are more concerned. Naturally one is always concerned with the form in any kind of statute; but we are more concerned with the changes in substance than we are with form. When changes in substance are involved we have been handling them in the department; and then when the substance goes into the law books in the form which we have given it, it is turned over to the other commission and they work it into their material in the manner which they think is proper.
