speechtext:
I am very glad my hon. friend speaks about history, because nobody seems to have any knowledge of the fundamentals of history in this House of Commons. If we speak history, people say that it is an unfair criticism-and I am not saying that with reference to the hon. member who has spoken, but rather with reference to a recent occurrence in the house, when everyone was shocked by the truth.
Canada is a place where we cannot tell the truth. But I try to; sometimes I am successful, and sometimes I am not.
But, Mr. Chairman, this may be very good legislation in the hands of a gentleman like the present minister; but it may be very bad legislation under a different minister; and it may be bad legislation with a good minister and a bad staff-as happened during the war in virtue of the defence regulations, when the leader of the opposition and Mr. Chaloult were both arrested, for nothing. The charge that was laid against the present leader of the opposition was withdrawn. Mr. Chaloult had to undergo trial before a judge, and he won.
The memory of some of the members of the press gallery is quite short. Two members of the press gallery were appointed censors, one being a former journalist and one an active member of the gallery. Both these men laid charges against a journalist
Criminal Code
from Toronto and a journalist from Montreal. I looked after the case and fortunately it was dropped. These two members of the press gallery, these two Judas Iscariots, tried to send to jail two of their confreres because they did not agree with the views of the leader of the government at that time.
I got in touch with the former minister of justice, Mr. Lapointe, and his secretary, both of whom are now dead. I got in touch also with the secretary of Mr. King, who is still alive. I wanted to make sure that those two journalists were not sent to jail. The minister of justice was in Portugal at the time.
Those two censors were awful. I hope the minister will see to it that nothing is done without his approval and in that case I feel sure everybody will have real security. Otherwise they will have none. If the administration of an act like that is left in the hands of bureaucrats no one will know who will be the first to suffer. That is why we must be very careful about it. I am not a protagonist of human rights and so-called fundamental freedoms, but I do not want my fellow citizens to be sent to jail without reason.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
I think hon. members will agree upon reflection that wherever an offence against this section 209 takes place it is desirable that if the accused is guilty he should not get off by reason of the crown's inability to bring home to him the act for which he is certainly responsible. Very often the crown when prosecuting under this section has been able to prove that the letter was sent through the mail because it was brought to them by the person who had received it through the mail, but it might be impossible to prove within the terms of

Criminal Code
the existing wording that the accused had! posted the letter. The present section reads:
Every one is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to two years' imprisonment who posts for transmission or delivery by or through the post any letter-
As I said a moment ago, we may be able to prove that he used the mails for the purpose of getting the letter to John Doe to whom it was addressed, and yet you may not be able to prove that he posted it. In 99 cases out of 100 he never would have posted it; it would have been posted by some person else. We are substituting words which we think will enable us to secure a conviction only in those cases in which a conviction should be secured. We think that in those cases in which a conviction should be secured we should not fail to get that conviction because we cannot prove that the accused posted the letter himself.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: No, I must confess that it has not. We received representations from British Columbia in this particular case. The British Columbia section of the Canadian Bar Association made the suggestion. I think they were actuated in making it by several rather nasty cases that had arisen in which, as my hon. friend knows is often the case, children were the victims of these sex perverts. They thought that by keeping them away from the places indicated in this section the purpose they had in mind might be served.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
The section is good as far as it goes. I think everyone will commend it. However, it is confined to cases of loitering or wandering in or near a school ground or playground. I should think there are other places which might well be included besides those two. One thinks of public parks. We had a case in Toronto not long ago where a horrible offence of this kind was committed in a park, which could not be classified, I think, as a school ground or playground. Playgrounds

have a specific connotation which would not be wide enough to include all parts of public parks.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: As my hon. friend can see, the principle of this section is the prevention of the loitering of these individuals in any place where children congregate in numbers. If my hon. friend would care to reflect upon the matter and would like to move an amendment adding some other place in addition to school grounds and playgrounds, I would be very glad to accept it because it would introduce no change in principle at all from that which is embodied in the section as it stands. We thought this pretty well covered it. One of the things you have to keep in mind is that we do not want to make it of such general application as to make it inoperative; but if my hon. friend, after we have gone through these other sections, would like to revert to this one and move an amendment adding one or two more places where children may congregate I would be very glad to accept it.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: Public parks occur to me.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext: There are adults in public parks whereas you do not see too many around schools. The first thing you know you will find that these people were better off in jail. I think it is a good step in the right direction, but let us not make it too confining or these people will almost be prisoners whether they are in or out. That is the difficulty as I see it. The thought is that there are children in great numbers around school grounds and playgrounds, and very few adults, but in parks you usually find older people and the difficulties do not arise in the same way.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
I must disagree with my hon. friend. Some of the worst cases we have had in my city have arisen in parks. I think far more of them have occurred in parks than in school grounds or playgrounds. Some playgrounds are located in public parks, but the expression "public park" would be much broader than playgrounds. My hon. friend indicates that many adults are usually to be found in the public parks. We have some pretty big public parks and the presence of adults in some of them has not prevented some of the worst of these offences being committed. In many cases playgrounds are supervised, but it is not possible to supervise all parts of the public parks. In the larger cities we have public parks that may run to several hundred acres.
Surely our first concern in a situation of this kind is not going to be the enjoyment of liberty on the part of people who have been convicted of the types of offences that
Criminal Code
are enumerated here. Mind you, Mr. Chairman, we are dealing here only with people who have already been convicted of these horrible offences against young girls. In a situation like this I am not going to waste very much concern on these people as to the abridgement of their right to loiter or hang around public parks. I am going to expend a good deal of concern on the young girls who may be using these parks for quite lawful purposes. I think we should be greatly concerned about protecting them from people who have been convicted of these sexual crimes against young girls. I cannot see any objection to the inclusion of public parks in the type of areas in which people convicted of these crimes are to be prevented from loitering or wandering. If they are going about their business and are not loitering or wandering they will not be committing an offence against this section, but if they are just hanging around, and, as we know from the newspapers, they hang around public parks a great deal, then they may be up to no good. I think that we ought to add public parks to the two areas in which these people are prohibited from loitering or wandering. I would urge that on the minister. It may be that on further reflection similar areas may occur to members of the house, but that is one that comes to my mind at once, and I would urge the minister to accept that addition.

speechtext:
This is the section dealing with drunken driving, and it is a most interesting experiment on the part of the department. It seems to me they are endeavouring to zone the law on drunken driving, and that by zoning the law they have actually reduced the danger to those who, being intoxicated, operate motorcars. Under the present section the minimum penalty on summary conviction is seven days and the maximum penalty is a period not exceeding thirty days. Because it is sometimes difficult to establish intoxication a junior offence has been created. This provides that everyone who, while his ability to drive a motor vehicle is impaired, drives such motor vehicle, is guilty of an offence. The penalty provided for a first offence is a fine not exceeding $500 and not less than $50 or imprisonment, or both fine and imprisonment.
I think in practice this will emasculate the drunken driving section in effect today and provide an easy escape for those who drive motor cars while intoxicated. Furthermore

Criminal Code
provision is made regarding chemical tests, urine tests, breath tests and so on; but on analysis of the section my submission is that it really amounts to very little. It provides that the result of a chemical analysis of the blood, urine, breath or other bodily substance may be admitted in evidence notwithstanding the fact that no warning was given. Then there is a further subsection stating that no person is required to give a sample of blood, urine, breath or other bodily substance for chemical analysis for the purposes of this section. In other words while it purports to extend the field within which the prosecution is able to secure evidence against an accused charged with driving while intoxicated, in fact it does not do so. All it provides is that such evidence may be admitted. Then, you come to the question whether or not it will be admitted. The giving of a warning that the accused does not have to submit is not necessary, but there are still many other reasons why the court would hold that what had been done had not been done voluntarily, and because of that the evidence would not be admissible. I think that while this section has a grandiloquent sound about it, in effect it is more show than it is actually helpful in meeting the situation.
I realize the difficulties. I did when I suggested on more than one occasion in the house that the breath test, the urine test and the blood test should be allowed. I realized that there would be an interference with the individual's rights by the taking of those tests. But drunken driving has become a serious matter menacing the lives of hundreds, if not thousands, of people within our country and requires very drastic action.
Mr. Justice Barlow of the trial court of Ontario, in January last, stated that of the seven manslaughter cases at the previous assizes in Toronto, each and every one of them had originated in the beer parlour. This indicates the degree of danger for persons properly using the highways, when they are brought in contact with those who operate cars when intoxicated. I am not going into the experience in other nations except by way of a quick reference. In Norway the provision is made that all drivers who have a blood alcohol concentration of -05 or over are considered guilty of an offence. There is a medical examination as well as an examination of the blood. In Sweden they have a combination of medical examination and chemical tests. There all those who have [DOT] 08 of alcohol in their blood are included, and those who have between -08 and -15, depending on the outcome of the clinical examination, are found either guilty or not
guilty. When it is found that the concentration of alcohol is over -15 per cent the person is guilty, regardless of the outcome of any chemical examination.
Recently the provincial directors of the Accident Prevention Association of Ontario met in conference in the city of Toronto. They dealt at length with the situation. They had authoritative speakers present on that occasion. Tests were made in Toronto in accidents involving personal injuries that had taken place over a period of time. It was found that in all the accidents that had taken place in Toronto that were investigated, twenty-three per cent of the drivers had more than a trace of alcohol in their blood. It further showed that the proportion of drivers that make errors in driving increase with the increasing concentration of alcohol from -05 to -14. It was also found that eighty-six per cent of all drivers having -15 per cent of alcohol in their blood had committed acts of driving negligence of one kind or another, which indicates that a percentage of -15 is a dangerous percentage for at least eighty-six per cent of all drivers operating motor cars. At this meeting at which there were toxicology representatives, and also enforcement officers, the final conclusion was that there was a definite relationship between the concentration of alcohol in the blood and driving errors resulting in accidents.
My submission is that this section, when read cursorily, indicates a serious endeavour is being made to provide for blood, urine and breath tests, whereas in fact the question is begged and not faced. I believe that the zoning of the law and the provision that is made now in the new subsection 4a, to which I have made reference, will have the result of increasing the number of convictions to no great extent, but will in fact be an invitation to drunken drivers and will result in a fine being imposed for the first offence rather than a prison sentence. While some may say that the possibility of seven days in jail is not a deterrent to those who would drive motorcars when in an advanced state of intoxication, nonetheless I think experience has shown-I am referring now to the evidence of police officers-that the fear of a minimum period of imprisonment has a deterrent effect. In fact, I believe the predecessor to the Minister of Justice stated on one occasion that an increase in the penalty providing for a greater minimum period of imprisonment would result in a greater degree of fear on the part of potential wrongdoers.
I am one of those who have always taken a strong stand on behalf of the liberty of the subject, and against any unnecessary invasion of his constitutional rights. But having regard

Criminal Code
to the mounting death rate in this country as a result of the driving of motor cars by intoxicated drivers, there is only one language that such potential wrongdoers understand and that is the stern enforcement of the law. Instead of revising the penalty to a mere fine with a minimum of $50, I would have thought there would have been an increase in the minimum period of imprisonment which now stands at seven days. Many may think that this new subsection 4d provides blood, urine, breath or other bodily tests, but it does not. It permits the court to admit such tests, but there is nothing to prevent the court from holding, whether or not a warning was given, that such an interference with the person of the alleged wrongdoer constitutes an invasion of his rights, and as such is inadmissible. Indeed, the wording of the section would seem to be an invitation to the court to hold that, except in unusual circumstances, such tests should not be admissible. I am going to say no more at this time but I feel that this section which, before it finally came before the house in its present form, had been proclaimed as a great forward step is in fact one that will do little or nothing to meet the increasing menace of homicide by drunken drivers whose regard for the rights of others diminishes in almost direct proportion to the degree to which they have imbibed intoxicating liquor. I should like to know who recommended the section in its present form, for it certainly does not go as far as the law enforcement officers would like it to go. Indeed, it constitutes but a mere faltering step forward in an aggressive campaign to protect the lives of our citizens from those who, by reason of their intoxication, care nothing for the rights of others.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rather feel
that, in joining in this debate, following the hon. member for Lake Centre, I am taking a great deal on my shoulders. I might say to the much more learned hon. member that I do think twice about doing so. Certainly if I object to any of the remarks he has made, he will recognize the fact that it is purely junior counsel doing so. I feel, however, that this section which is proposed to be put into the code is a good one, as far as I see it. From practice as I myself know it, I think it would be a much greater deterrent to driving while drunk than is the present section in the code. I feel that if magistrates have this section to use they will be much more inclined to convict than they will be if they are obliged to operate under the present section. I say that with all due respect to my hon. and learned friend who has had infinitely more experience in larger spheres 
than I have. But I myself feel that this is a good section, and I would want it to stay there.
I agree with him-and I am not quite certain that he spoke altogether as I feel about the other important section having to do with the invasion of the rights of the subject, in connection with this question of the testing of the various processes of the human body. I feel strongly about that matter, Mr. Chairman. With all due respect to those who drafted this section, I feel that a warning should be given by the arresting constable, or whoever does the arresting, before such a test is made. I do not think it is right or proper that these tests should be merely taken as a matter of course without the arrested person being properly warned that he need not be subject to a test if he does not wish to have it.
From the little knowledge that I have of these things, I see how a grave injustice could be done. Certainly it is contrary to the principles of British justice as I know it. As I say, if my hon. and learned friend had spoken in a contrary fashion-and I am not quite certain whether he has or has not-I agree with him. If he has not, I disagree with him. I think that provision should be included. I think a warning should be given before any man has to undergo a test of any of these types that are set forth in this act.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
I just want to bring one
situation to the minister's attention. While I am in general agreement with this section, it seems to me that the mandatory imprisonment for drunken driving-particularly drunken driving which has resulted in an accident-should be clearly stated in the Criminal Code. I mention this point in view of an accident that happened here in Ottawa only a few days ago, where a driver had not only one accident but two, and where he nearly killed one of the surveyors working for either the city of Ottawa or the parks commission, as I gather. He left the scene of the accident, leaving the surveyor or the engineer prone on the ground, having destroyed his transit, changed cars, got into a taxi and when he was picked up

through what must be considered to be a bright piece of work on the part of a policeman-was found to be in an advanced stage of intoxication. The driver was fined $500. That man might easily have killed somebody. In fact, he seriously injured a surveyor. Had he gone up and hit him on the head with a hammer or, in other words, assaulted him, he would certainly have been imprisoned for bodily assault. But because he hit somebody with a motorcar, he is fined $500.

Criminal Code
I am not a lawyer, but it seems to me that it is just as dangerous and just as bad for a driver, when drunk, to drive a motorcar over a man as it is to go up and assault him on the street. It seems to me that the section should have a clause providing for mandatory imprisonment for this sort of accident.
In my opinion the thing which causes as much in the way of accidents as I have seen is the insulting behaviour of motorists to each other, the insulting behaviour of motorists to pedestrians and vice versa. I do not suppose it could be possible that some clause could be put in the code with regard to insulting language used by motorists to each other. Nothing is so likely to adversely affect the driving ability of a motorist who is in charge of a heavy and powerful machine which is capable of causing death in a split second as the impairment of his judgment; and there is nothing that is more likely to impair a driver's judgment than anger. I do not suppose it would be possible to have such a clause in the section. There is the old saying about care and courtesy. It is a question of courtesy in driving, something which is of inestimable importance to safety and security on our roads.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
I should like to say a few words in explanation of the government's position in this matter, my doubts as to whether or not I should do so having been set at rest by getting a note from one of my colleagues who indicated that his constituents would like to have something on record-and I am sure this may be true of others-as to the basis upon which the government has proceeded in this legislation. This matter came up last year, and at that time, if my memory serves me correctly- and Hansard seems to indicate that it does- the hon. member for Lake Centre was strongly in favour of some of the types of chemical tests that had been employed in American jurisdictions, Michigan in particular, as having very greatly improved the law enforcement there.
Improvement in law enforcement depends to some extent upon the condition of law enforcement at the time the improvement began; and it may be that conclusions based upon the improvements which took place in Michigan would not be tenable as applied to the law enforcement in the Canadian provinces.
I might add, by way of compliment, if I may put it that way, in respect of the hon. member's remarks of last year, that the government took his views seriously, and that since that time we have had one of the abler
members of our staff go into the matter carefully. He went to Detroit and examined the improvements they had made there. He went to Chicago and to Northwestern University at Evanston. Then he came back and found, according to a report he made to us, that the best work of all in his opinion was that being carried on by the department of pharmacology of the university of Toronto. Portions of my remarks tonight are based in large measure upon a report which Dr. H. W. Smith of the department of pharmacology prepared at our request on this subject. We, in turn, have given support to some important research into the problem at the university of Toronto, by means of a grant from the Department of National Health and Welfare.
As a result of these surveys we have conducted we feel we have obtained all the information available in Canada which is likely to have a bearing upon the problem, and it is on the basis of this information which we have secured that the present proposals now before hon. members are made.
What is the main purpose of legislation directed against driving after drinking? Surely it is to eliminate drinking as a cause of motor accidents and motor deaths. For example, this mandatory punishment of seven days in jail, in addition to the impoundment of the car for some months, which is visited upon an otherwise respectable citizen who has been guilty of driving while drunk, is infinitely more severe than any punishment that the law imposes upon him for merely being drunk. And the reason why that serious punishment is inflicted upon him, the reason for the extra heavy penalty, is to prevent the accidents and deaths which are caused by drunken driving.
The next important question is, I think: When does the consumption of alcohol affect a driver so that he is more likely to have an accident than if he had not been drinking? The answer to this question we have received, from inquiries we have made of these scientific gentlemen, is that a driver is dangerous, not merely when he is completely drunk. Indeed, if he is sufficiently drunk his danger to traffic has disappeared, because he cannot drive his car at all.
It is now scientifically established that alcohol will impair the efficiency of a driver so that he does not drive at all with his normal ability, even though the degree to which he is under the influence of liquor may fall short of complete intoxication.
In other words scientists say that, short of intoxication, alcohol has two nutjor effects

Criminal Code
which lead to accidents. The first is what they call euphoria, or a sense of false confidence, amounting in some cases almost to irresponsibility. The second is a physical effect by way of a slowing up of the reflexes or the reaction time of the driver. Short of complete intoxication, alcohol will bring about a serious impairment in the ability of the driver, as a result of these two influences.
The hon. member has asked who recommended this. Well, what we have produced is the result of the deliberations of the cabinet itself. But in those deliberations we did have the views of these scientific men. And in their view an important objective of legislation against driving after drinking would be to prohibit driving, not only when the driver is completely intoxicated, but when his ability to drive has been seriously impaired by the consumption of alcohol. And I imagine the case cited tonight by the hon. member for York West of, as he said, an assault by automobile was probably the result of the actions of a man whose ability to drive had been impaired by the consumption of alcohol.
It is to take care of that kind of driving that this new section has been inserted in the Criminal Code. And, if this is any reassurance to the hon. member for Lake Centre, it has the endorsement of those who have studied this matter from a scientific standpoint. Also if I understood the hon. member for Lake Centre correctly-and I hope he will correct me if I am wrong-I gathered from his remarks last year that in his opinion one of the reasons why there were not more convictions for drunken driving in Canada, in proportion to the amount of drunken driving which he said was taking place in this country, was that because of the mandatory jail sentence the police, the prosecutors and, in particular, the magistrates hesitated to prosecute and convict an accused person because they knew he would have to go to jail if such a finding was made. For a man who was otherwise respectable this was a very great odium. Because of that what happened was-and my hon. friend told us this repeatedly; I am sure he will recollect it -that they laid charges of reckless driving, and not drunken driving at all.
He brought forward that argument in opposition to my contention that the law as it stood at that time, and as it stands now, before this new amendment comes into effect, was quite capable of enforcement if the authorities would just get busy and enforce it. We thought that in providing a new offence of driving while one's ability to drive was impaired by alcohol or drugs, we were not only creating what perhaps should have been an offence before-because it is the 
driving of that sort of persons which has injured many innocent people in this country -but we were also providing, for that group of reckless driving cases to which my hon. friend referred, a means whereby these gentlemen whose drinking had resulted in something less than intoxication, could be brought to justice without having to use the device of charging reckless driving.
While it is quite true that for the first offence under this new section the penalty is a fine of $50, for the second offence under this section there is a mandatory provision for imprisonment, just as under .the drunken driving provision.

speechtext:
You really need an aroused public opinion.
Mr. Garson,: Quite so. My hon. friend is entirely right. In every one of these jurisdictions where the authorities were doing a good job of prosecuting to conviction drunken drivers there had been a condition precedent of an aroused public opinion that put the authorities right on the spot. They had no other choice but to go ahead with a policy of strict law enforcement.
We must remember that we are making laws for the whole of Canada. In order to preserve it for those provinces in which there was adequate enforcement under the law as it stands at the present time and with existing methods of proof we retained upon the statute books the existing charge of drunken driving. We do not put the authorities, in rural areas for instance where they could not provide chemical tests-we do not confront them with the necessity of having in all cases

to provide chemical tests. They can proceed in the same way they are doing now to secure a conviction on the charge of drunken driving without any change from the practice they have been following up to the present time.
But in those other places where the local authorities claim, rightly or wrongly, that they find it impossible to do what is being done in some provinces, that they are embarrassed because of this mandatory jail sentence and cannot get convictions, we have provided this other offence of driving while one's ability to drive is impaired. This offence not only stands up on its own merits but also provides the authorities in those areas, mostly metropolitan areas, who claim they have difficulty enforcing the present law, with a means whereby they can bear down upon those who are driving motor cars through our streets after they have been indulging too heavily in the cup that cheers.
I may say a word with regard to chemical tests-I hope my hon. friend from Lake Centre will correct me if I am wrong, and I shall be glad to read back to him from Hansard what he said although I do not think that is necessary-I got the impression that the kind of chemical test he would favour was the one in which the crown or the state, as it would be in the United States, or along the lines that he quoted in Norway and Sweden, would come in with evidence to indicate that a man's blood test or breath test or saliva test or urine test showed a certain percentage of alcohol; and that by that one fact that the accused had a certain percentage of alcohol in his bodily substance, a statutory presumption would be raised against him which he would have to rebut. In other words, instead of the prosecution having to prove that he was guilty, instead of his being innocent until he was proven guilty, by the operation of that particular kind of chemical test the position would be reversed, and the onus would then shift to the accused of proving that he was innocent.

speechtext:
What we have provided in this bill is, first, no more than a statutory enactment which will make applicable to all 80709-297
Criminal Code
provinces in Canada the effect of the Ontario court of appeal decision which was that if a chemical test of alcohol concentration in the blood is taken without warning it is admissible in evidence. Thus we say in our legislation here that evidence as to the alcoholic content of the accused's blood is admissible for whatever probative value it may have in the opinion of the court, and that no special significance attaches to any particular alcoholic concentration in the blood but that that must be considered by the court along with all other clinical evidence in deciding whether the accused was driving a car while his ability to drive was impaired, or while he was intoxicated.
There are a number of reasons for this legislation taking the form it has. Some of them are in favour of the crown and the others are in favour of the accused. One of the results which flow from what took place in some of these United States jurisdictions which my hon. friend seems to admire so much is this: When you bring evidence into court that a man has, we will say, [DOT] 15 per cent alcoholic content in his blood, and when you provide by statute that upon proof of that fact-this appears to be the case in some Scandinavian countries-a man shall be convicted, he is in effect being convicted out of a test tube. If he has that percentage of alcohol concentration he is guilty of the offence.
That also means that the man who has just less than that is proved to be sober, is proved to be innocent. You cannot create a standard of drunkenness or impairment without automatically creating a standard of nonintoxication or non-impairment just under the other. And the line that separates guilt from innocence on this basis is perhaps two ten-thousandths or -02 per cent. All the scientists seem to agree that impairment starts at around -05 per cent, which is not quite one two-thousandth part in volume.

speechtext:
My hon. friend will be able to see his views on that very point. Impairment commences at a blood concentration of -05 per cent in persons who are very sensitive to alcohol, and then in the case of persons who are resistant there will be a spread from this -05 per centum or -08 per cent up to this point of -13 per cent. That means that while science can determine what percentage of alcohol in the blood will cause impairment

Criminal Code
in a sensitive person and what will cause impairment in a very resistant person, it cannot be said with regard to John Doe, who is somewhere in between, whether he is or is not impaired on the basis of the blood test alone. If the hon. member for Lake Centre will examine all of Dr. Ward Smith's material he will see that in a very elaborate series of studies involving some 16,000 subjects conducted in Europe, some scientists who conducted them were of the view that a blood concentration of [DOT] 15 per cent indicated intoxication; others that -45 per cent, three times as great, constituted intoxication; and still others at varying percentages between these extremes.
What is the explanation of this variation? The explanation of the variation arises from the definition of intoxication. The scientists who claimed that -45 per cent was required to establish intoxication adopted a series of symptoms, gross staggering, flushed face, lack of co-ordination, in other words, a very advanced state of intoxication. The scientists who claimed that -15 per cent would produce intoxication adopted as their standard of intoxication merely that the subject drove a car more recklessly than ninety per cent of a normal group of drivers. One can see from that that the figure of [DOT] 45 proceeded from a set of premises. Once it was assumed that intoxication meant gross, serious intoxication, then it followed inevitably from that that a high blood alcohol concentration was required to produce that intoxication. Once you adopted a low degree of intoxication as indicating drunkenness, then a low alcoholic concentration would produce that drunkenness.
In other words, the scientists in reaching their conclusions as to the blood concentration which was required to establish intoxication were using for the standard upon which their logic was based the same kind of clinical symptoms that the village constable would use in proving a case of drunkenness before the village magistrate, that the person staggered, that his face was flushed, that his speech was slurred, that he had lost co-ordination, and so on, and one result flowed from the other. This scientific evidence has no magic to it. It should go into the case and be considered-and in this I am happy to note that the hon. member for Lake Centre agrees with our viewpoint-as one of the facts to be taken into consideration along with all other facts in arriving at the decision as to whether or not in that case the accused was drunk, or whether or not his ability to drive was impaired. But even on that basis it is of very great value because it will negative those cases in which the accused says that he took too many aspirins, that he was shocked by the [Mr. Garsor '
accident or was upset because he had run over some person, and that he was not intoxicated at all, that he was not impaired at all, that it was just these circumstances and not his consumption of alcohol, perish the thought, which had confounded him. The blood test likewise will indicate if the alcohol concentration is low that it may be because the man is ill, or is tired, or his stomach is empty, that he is in trouble, and then it will operate in his defence.
What we have done is that we have tried to retain all the workable and good features of the law as it stands at the present time. We have tried to add to the offences a new one of driving while one's ability to drive is impaired, which is quite sound on its own basis, and which, judging by the representations we have received from the police forces and others in the larger centres, will enable them to deal with a whole multitude of cases which they say they cannot deal with now.
We have provided for chemical tests. They are not compulsory. They do not set up any presumption against the accused. We are still a British country and a man is still innocent until he is proven guilty. The burden is still on the crown of proving him guilty from start to finish. The result of all this is that we think we have retained all the existing benefits and added to them what we hope will prove to be fairly pronounced improvements.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
I think if there is any virtue
in this measure-and I have no doubt there is-it lies in something that has been going on in this country for some years, preventive medicine. I think that is the real virtue in this amendment to the Criminal Code. If a person is found under these conditions and convicted the fine may be only $50 for the first offence, but if he is convicted a second time it means three months' imprisonment, and I would think that would be a fair warning. I do not know whether this provision will add very much. Usually the matter of drunkenness is taken into consideration when a person is charged with reckless driving, outside of a charge of drunken driving, and so far as I know it has always been the law in my province that a judge is entitled to tell a jury that if a man is less capable of driving his car on account of taking liquor than he would be if he had taken no liquor at all that indicates negligence, and gross negligence at that.
Of course this goes a step further. A man may be convicted of this offence for his inability to drive because of taking too much liquor, if liquor has that effect on him, but I think the crown is going to have tremendous difficulty in proving these cases at

all. I think the only way you can prove that a man is less capable of driving on account of liquor than he would be if he had none at all is by his actions. When it comes to the tests that are made, liquor has a different effect on thousands of people. That was brought out in the remarks of the Minister of Justice. For example, everybody that has had anything to do with these matters knows that there are some people who can take six good glasses of whisky and it has no more effect on them than if they had taken two glasses of water. You have got to go into all that. You have to go into the psychology of the individual, the effect liquor may have on him and all that kind of thing; and I am afraid the amendment is not going to do too much good except, as I say, by way of prevention. Personally I would rather have seen this amendment deferred until Mr. Justice Martin of the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia, who has had a tremendous amount of experience in this matter, brought down the results of his investigation.
Suppose a man has a blood test. Who is going to prove what effect the liquor he has taken has had upon his ability to drive? Toronto university has carried out some investigations into this matter. Well, unless they get a doctor who agrees with the results of those investigations, they will have to take the men who carried out the investigations to various parts of the country, because there are as many opinions in the medical profession as to the effects of alcohol as there are on other questions of this kind. I think the trouble will be in the proof. Drunken driving cases never came before the court over which I had the honour to preside for some years, but in any case where the evidence would make an ordinary person feel that a man was drunk and practically incapable of driving a car I believe the magistrates of our province have carried out their duty and responsibility. Personally I think that as far as manslaughter is concerned it was a mistake to give the court power to tell the jury that if they did not find the accused guilty of manslaughter they could find him guilty of reckless driving. The very basis of manslaughter is reckless driving. If a man is driving recklessly and the car over which he has control kills someone, that is absolute proof of manslaughter. I understand that change was put through for certain reasons which came from the province of Ontario. I have tried a good many cases of manslaughter, and I can remember only one in which the accused was not found guilty when there was evidence that he was driving recklessly. Sometimes the trouble with our courts is that the juries are not told what
80709-297J
Criminal Code
recklessness means. If I am driving a car slowly but looking up at the tall buildings or something of the kind I am just as reckless as though I were driving a hundred miles an hour.
I am getting away from the subject under discussion. I believe the virtue of this amendment will be in prevention. Once you get a conviction under this new section I believe it will help prevent this sort of thing, but I do not see how you are going to get a conviction on scientific evidence alone. I feel quite sure it will be practically an impossibility. It is easy enough to have a man found guilty of drunken driving with the aid of scientific evidence, but I think you will find tremendous difficulties in connection with this new provision.
There is just one other point on which I want to say a word. The section includes the words "or has the care or control of a motor vehicle or automobile, whether it is in motion or not". The only way to prove whether a man is up to snuff, as the saying goes, is the way he drives. How are you going to prove that his ability to drive is below par because of liquor if he is just sitting in the car at the side of the road? I do not see how that is going to help in the matter of proof.

maintopic: VARIOUS AMENDMENTS RELATING TO OFFENSIVE WEAPONS, PENALTY FOR OFFENCES OF A SEDITIOUS NATURE, IMPROPER USE OF MAILS, ETC.
speechtext:
I find myself very much in sympathy with what has been said by the hon. member for Lake Centre, and thinking very much along the lines of the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond. I do not see how you are ever going to get sufficient evidence to prove your case under the new section. As has been pointed out already, liquor evidently has as many different effects upon human beings as there are human beings, and I doubt that any scientist could possibly determine the effect upon the ability of a given man to drive. However, that is not the point I rose to discuss. I am just a bit puzzled about the relationship between the two subsections, 4 and 4a. First I would like to know undier which of these subsections a charge would be laid. From some speakers I have understood that the new subsection is supposed to be not only a new classification but also something of a lesser infraction of the law. Would the minister say just how a peace officer would proceed to lay a charge and under which subsection a charge would be laid, because both will be in the act? Following that I would like to ask how the penalty range for a first offence was arrived at. In subsection 4 as it now stands the penalty is imprisonment for from thirty days to three months. Under the new subsection the penalty range is a fine of from $50 to $500 or a jail term of up to three months, or both.

Criminal Code
In case a judge decided to impose both fine and imprisonment the maximum could be a fine of $500 and imprisonment for three months. That does not suggest a lesser infraction of the law by any means. So I would like to know how the penalty range was arrived at in the two subsections.

speechtext:
I wonder if this is not what would happen. A policeman brings in a man he has found in charge of a motor vehicle and in a condition of insobriety. The constable will recount what the scientists call his clinical symptoms, that is his conduct; whether he speaks in a slurring way, whether he staggers, and what other indications of insobriety he may show. Under the law as it now stands, without any chemical tests at all, the gentleman who is in charge of the booking-I have not had enough experience to know the proper term for the man who is in charge of the police station- will decide, from what evidence he can get, whether he thinks they can make a charge of drunken driving stick against this accused. If they think they can do so they will lay this charge. When the case comes up in court, the crown witnesses, the policeman who took him in charge and any crown witnesses they have who saw the occurrence -perhaps he collided with a lamp post or maybe he drove through a traffic signal- will state the facts that have a bearing on the case. The court will hear what they have to say, and hear any defence that the accused puts in, then decide whether it thinks he was intoxicated while in charge of that motorcar.
When this bill is passed, in addition to the other evidence, they may have a chemical test showing he had an alcohol concentration in his blood of say -18 per cent. That would be evidence corroborating the clinical symptoms to which the policeman testified, and make rather convincing corroborative evidence. This would be a case of drunken driving.
But suppose the man were not completely intoxicated. He has been involved in an accident, his breath smells of liquor but he can walk fairly straight. He appears to be somewhat under the influence of liquor. Then, if they have a test and it indicates his blood concentration is not -18 per cent but only [DOT]08 per cent they would upon the prosecution of the accused place all the facts before the court and it would be for the court to decide whether that man's ability to drive was impaired by his consumption of alcohol. The chemical test would show the reason for the impairment. There it is. There is an indication of what he had in his blood. The fact

that he ran into this other car under circumstances which indicated it was his fault indicates some impairment of his driving ability. From these facts that are submitted to the court, the court has to decide whether it regards his ability to drive as having been impaired on that occasion. If it is felt that the case has not been established there is an acquittal. If it is felt that the case has been established there is a conviction. I think it is just as simple as that. If the accused does not think that is fair, he can take an appeal to a higher court. I think perhaps from unfamiliarity with the new offence, and also perhaps because impairment is a less definite condition than drunkenness, it may be more difficult, but it will work itself out.

speechtext: Let me assure the Minister of Justice, and the member for Lake Centre, that I certainly sympathize with every effort that has been made to reduce the accidents and the terrible things that do happen as a result of people trying to drive a motorcar while they are under the influence of liquor. speechtext:
I am rather disappointed that there has not been incorporated in these amendments some arrangement to require chronic alcoholics to go to a hospital and take treatment for chronic alcoholism. The province of Ontario has made progressive studies in this regard recently, I believe, based on research by Yale university. Whereas formerly alcoholism was considered a disgrace, I believe that today it is generally recognized

as a disease that can be, if not cured, at least checked. I should like to recommend to the Minister of Justice that some time amendments be incorporated making it compulsory, say on the fourth conviction for drunken driving, that the accused be hospitalized and the cure for alcoholism taken.
You would not be taking away the rights of the citizen. We have compulsory hospitalization for tuberculosis. A man is taken out of society if he is a carrier of disease. Certainly the drunken driver is far more dangerous when seated at the wheel of a car than the carrier of a contagious disease, such as measles or diphtheria. We have antidotes for those, but we have no antidotes for the drunken driver. I think it is worth serious consideration. If you sentence a man to jail time and time again for drunken driving or common drunkenness, his first reaction when he gets out is to get drunk again. We have all seen that happen time and time again. You can take a man's driving licence away from him, but you cannot keep him from driving a car if he is a certain type of drunkard. He will get behind the wheel of a car, and then he is a maniac who is a potential murderer.
The province has been getting large profits out of the liquor business, so I would recommend that the province establish units to which a chronic alcoholic could go for treatment in order to be reclaimed as a useful citizen, instead of being thrown into jail and treated as a common jailbird. Such treatment is not doing him one bit of good, and still leaves him a potential maniac on the highways.

Mr. Chairman, this is the section that introduces into our law a form of wire tapping. This section, the minister stated

this afternoon, had been requested by the attorney general of one of the provinces, or by the department of the attorney general, and this is the type of thing to which I believe the house should take most strenuous objection.
Some weeks ago in the course of a general discussion in the house I stated I was unalterably opposed to the principle of wire tapping. This section introduces a type of wire tapping, while the tapping does not actually permit of information being secured-or, in fact, denies it.
This section is one of those things that border on the sort of thing one expects in a police state, and must be guarded against. I had occasion today to look up the discussion in the United States which took place some years ago during the days of war, in reference to the whole problem of wire tapping. President Roosevelt summed up the situation when he said that the great problem today is to balance the need for law enforcement with the need for the protection of citizens against the abuse of such powers.
I do not think it has been before our supreme court; but the Supreme Court of the United States has spoken about wire tapping in language that could be understood. Now, I think certain questions arise. One of them is this: Have betting houses and common gambling houses become so widespread that they are undermining this nation? Certainly there is no evidence of it; and I cannot believe that conditions such as were revealed by the Kefauver commission are in existence in this country. In the United States it was shown that the law authorities and the underworld were operating together in various cities in connection with gambling and gaming houses, and common betting houses, to the detriment of democracy.
Even if you answer that question in the affirmative, it does not settle the matter; because liberty is never more in danger than it is when those who are well meaning, but who have no appreciation of what liberty means, by insidious means introduce things which though innocent in themselves ultimately bring about those things that characterize the police state.
This section looks innocent. It merely allows police officers to sit in and watch telephone calls in order to ascertain the degree to which the telephone is being used. But if we begin to allow police officers to do this, we take the first step along the lines toward the most intolerable abuses that can possibly be imagined, namely interference with the
Criminal Code
privacy of individuals by the totally inexcusable method of wire tapping, and by kindred means.
It is all very well to say that under this section wire tapping in itself is not going to be allowed. If we permit this to pass, it will constitute a precedent, and it will not be a long step, once this precedent has been established, for the state to ask for the legalization of the right to snoop into the private business and affairs of any individual in this country.
I know of nothing that arouses my personal antagonism more than the step being asked for by parliament, as provided for in this section. It looks innocent; but it is a step that can only lead to the desire of law officers to go the whole way and deny freedom of communication and the right of privacy.

Business of the House before the house, and there are obvious reasons why it is desirable that one department, which only has a comparatively few items, and can be dealt with in a short time, should be held back.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
The explanation is
the following: We have three days to move to go into supply and to call departments that have not been called. They are Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday.
This is the last department. If we move to go into supply we intend to call that department of legislation. Even if we go into supply on Wednesday we still would have to make a formal motion, and grievances could be brought up. I do not see that there is much difference.
Then on Thursday, Friday and Saturday we do not need a formal motion.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: I think it would be an advantage if it is deferred at least until Wednesday.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Will the hon. member undertake that if we do go into supply and do not call this department there will not be any debate?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: All right; we call the department.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
But I would point out that if the government leader in the house is anxious to expedite business he might well reconsider

the advisability of calling this remaining department, because I should think it should be fairly obvious to him that he might delay the consideration of other matters now before the house which perhaps could be dealt with in an orderly procedure tomorrow.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: My hon. friend knows that I always co-operate. We will call that department because if there is going to be a debate on going into supply I cannot see the usefulness of saying that we will not call it. If I had the assurance of the hon. gentleman that we would go into supply at a certain time during the day and take up transport or national defence I would be ready to forgo that and call this department on Wednesday; but if there is to be a debate one way or the other I am not losing anything.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: In view of the interest of the government and the house in expediting the business of the session would it not be a good idea to let the Judges Act amending bill stay over until the fall session?

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: It is rather contentious.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
The bill was
announced and I have to say that the government has decided to proceed with it.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Tuesday. June 26. 1951
